settlement legislation.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: I thank the Leader of the
House for that update. I just wonder whether he could confirm that when we reach the
next members’ day, the Government will ensure speedy progress to allow Sue
Moroney’s Parental Leave and Emplo yment Protection (Six Months’ Paid Leave)
Amendment Bill to have the airing in the House it deserves.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: That is a rather confusing
request to come from the shadow Leader of the House. I note that yesterday the
Opposition, in fact, stalled the day by asking questions to members and, further, put in a
letter to the Speaker seeking an additional hour -long special debate. Then, after years of
saying this is the fastest-legislating Government in the West, it said we need to actually
stop going quickly or go even more quickly. So what is the position of the Opposition?
Does it want good legislation or not?
Oil and Gas Exploration—2014 Block Offer and Conservation Land
1. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co -Leader—Green) to the Minister of Energy and

items.speaker: Resources
items.text: Does he think conservation land, des ignated as ecological areas, should be
opened up for petroleum exploration as part of Block Offer 2014?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Yes, and, as the
member knows, any operator wanting to undertake exploration activity within these
areas would need to first meet all the regulatory requirements, including obtaining an
access agreement from the Department of Conservation and resource consent under the
Resource Management Act from the relevant local authority. Let us remember that the
block offer is a call for exploration bids, and that exploration itself is just the first step
in a long process that may or may not lead to production.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Is he aware that the Conservation Act, which applies to all
Ministers, says that every designated ecological area “shall so be managed as to protect
the value for which it is held.”?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Is he aware that the  Orikaka Ecological Area was created to
protect important great spotted kiwi habitat, and how is allowing bulldozers to rip open
this area to pave the way for gigantic drilling rigs protecting the value of this sp ecial
place?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I am glad that the member can name an ecological area,
because on radio this morning he could not.
17170 Questions for Oral Answer 10 Apr 2014

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Answer the question. [ Interruption] Order! I invite the
Minister to answer the question.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: But we take these issues very seriously. That is why I said
in my primary answer that there is a layered process, which this is merely the beginning
of. The sort of issues that Mr Norman is raising will  be processed and considered by the
Department of Conservation and also through the Resource Management Act process.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Is he aware that the Kaniere Ecological Area was created to
protect dense rimu hill forest and habitat  for long-finned eels and short -jawed kōkopu,
and how is allowing bulldozers to rip open this area to pave the way for gigantic drilling
rigs protecting the value of this special designated place?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I am not aware of th at. It could be one of the ecological
areas that the Labour Party consented when it was in Government, and when Mr
Norman’s party was propping it up.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Is he aware that the Te Wharau Ecological Area was created to
protect a relatively isolated pākihi and mānuka shrub land ecosystem and a fernbird
population, and how is allowing bulldozers to rip open this area to pave the way for
gigantic drilling rigs protecting the special value of this special designated place?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON B RIDGES
items.text: I will just speak to the member. It strikes me that this is
scaremongering by the member, simply because that is a party that says no to all
development, no ifs, no buts. Actually this is a party on this side of the House, and on
its better days—

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The Minister is making no
attempt to address the question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I agree. The member will repeat the question for the benefit of the
Minister.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Is he aware that the Te Wharau E cological Area was created to
protect a relatively isolated p ākihi and m ānuka shrub  land ecosystem and a fernbird
population, and how is allowing bulldozers to rip open this area to pave the way for
gigantic drilling rigs protecting the special value of this special designated place?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I am not aware of any of the emotive claptrap that the
member is talking about.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Is he aware that the Mount Hārata  Ecological Area was created
to protect unmodified red beech - dominant forests and wildlife habitats that are
particularly important to birds, and how is allowing bulldozers to rip open this area to
pave the way for gigantic drilling rigs protecting the value of this special designated and
legislatively protected place?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I refer the member essentially to my earlier response to
the last supplementary question. But I think it is worth understanding here that
ecological areas in this block offer are entirely on the West Coast. The West Coast has
had mining and conservation coexisting, for the most part harmoniously, for well over
100 years. There has been consenting in ecological areas under both the National
Government and the last Labour Government, which the Green Party propped up and
did nothing to stop.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Will he respect the wishes of New Zealanders who love our
precious places and wildlife, not to mention the Conservation Act, by re fusing to grant
petroleum exploration permits over any designated ecological areas?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Absolutely. That is why under this Government a third of
New Zealand is conservation estate and 13 percent is schedule 4. We have a v ery clear
policy that we are not touching any of that. In relation to the other parts of the
conservation estate that are not in schedule 4, as I made clear in my answer to the
primary question, we have absolutely got robust processes, through the Departme nt of

Conservation and through the Resource Management Act processes, post the very start
of it—which is exploration, indeed, that we have consulted on.
Economy—IMF Reports and Impact of Economic Inequality
2. Hon DAVID PARKER (Deputy Leader —Labour) to the Minister of Finance:
Does he believe that the Government’s policies have reduced income inequality; if so,
does he agree with the IMF that rising inequality slows economic growth?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The evidence shows that inequality in
New Zealand has been flat or slightly declining since the mid -2000s. We also believe
that a number of the measures the  Government took through the recession certainly
prevented inequality from worsening at a time when the Government was very short of
revenue. But I welcome the member’s interest in the IMF’s view, because among its
recent comments on New Zealand, the IMF e mphasised the importance of ongoing
fiscal discipline to a sustainable economic recovery. Nowhere in the statement does the
IMF refer to inequality, and that is for a very good reason in respect of New Zealand —
that inequality in New Zealand has not increased over the last 10 years.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Well, then, do I take it that the Budget that is upcoming will
reverse the 40 percent of the 2010 income tax cuts that went to the top 10 percent of
income earners?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No. If the member bothered doing his homework, he would
have seen that at the time of the 2010 tax package, we published detailed distributional
impact measures, which showed—

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: Must be rubbish.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No. Those measures showed that the combination of income
tax cuts and an increase in GST and, effectively, a billion -dollar increase in property
taxes meant that that tax package was distributionally neutral.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Is he so out of touch that he thinks that inequality is not getting
worse, when 74 percent of New Zealanders believe that the gap between rich and poor
has increased under his Government, or does he side with the 3 percent who think that
the gap has narrowed?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: That member may be a stranger to the facts, but I am not.
The measuring system of the previous Government, which, I understand, was a Labour
Government, was such that regular reporting on inequality was carried out by highly
qualified professionals. That is the information on which we relied for the statement that
inequality in New Zealand has not got worse in the last few years.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Everyone else is wrong.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I accept that some people believe that. The fact is it is not
correct.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I seek leave to table the results of the Herald-DigiPoll, which
showed that 74 percent of New Zealand—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Th e point has been made. The Herald-DigiPoll is available
to all members.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: How can he justify being out of touch with the 74 percent of
New Zealanders who say that inequality has increased when homeownership has
declined to its lowest rate in 50 years under his watch?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I am not sure the member is correct about the
homeownership figures, but in any case we look for—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: They got worse under Labour.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, under Labour house prices doubled, which probably
did not help. But despite the severe damage Labour caused to the housing market, we
would like to see the Opposition parties support Government efforts to increase the
17172 Questions for Oral Answer 10 Apr 2014
supply of housing by helping us persuade councils to allow more new houses to be built
more quickly.

items.speaker: Louise Upston
items.text: What recent reports has he received from the IMF on the New
Zealand economy?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The most re cent report from the IMF did not refer to
inequality as a constraint on growth, for the very good reason that inequality in New
Zealand has not worsened. It did note that New Zealand has broad -based economic
growth and increasing business and consumer conf idence. It said that the Government’s
fiscal management and monetary policy has helped to deliver improved resilience
against future shocks to the economy. It considers that the steps taken by the
Government to alleviate housing supply bottlenecks will eas e pressures in the housing
market, and in the long run, I believe, those steps will help to ease inequality in New
Zealand, because one of the biggest drivers of inequality is the high cost of housing.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Does he deny tha t the current annual student turnover rate at
decile 1 primary schools, which is a shocking 52.8 percent per annum, is a further
symptom of rising inequality, and is this further evidence supporting the findings of the
OECD that inequality is having a major and negative impact on educational outcomes in
New Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, I do not agree with all of that. The interesting thing
about the OECD work is that it shows that economic inequality in New Zealand has
among the lowest levels of impact because of our education system. Part of the reason
for having public education —in fact, the main reason —is to overcome the inequalities
of birth and inequalities of opportunity. That is why this Government is so strongly
focused on helpin g our system be more effective in overcoming economic inequality.
Another reason there is high transience in those schools is that the State housing system
does not meet the needs of those with serious housing need. That is why the
Government is changing that policy next week.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Why can the Minister not see that rising inequality under
National goes against the egalitarian values that New Zealanders hold dear, is making
educational outcomes worse, and is holding back economic growth?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: There is a very simple reason we do not believe those things,
despite the fact that the member does, and that is that the measures of inequality in New
Zealand and the facts demonstrate that it has not got w orse. That is not a political
assertion or an ideological conviction; it is the facts as laid out in the annual report from
the Ministry of Social Development, which was set in place by the previous
Government. On “Planet Labour” I know facts have very lit tle impact, but on Planet
Earth and in New Zealand the facts matter.

items.speaker: Louise Upston
items.text: What comments has the International Monetary Fund made
previously about the New Zealand economy?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: In the light of recent discussion about the history of the New
Zealand economy, I looked for the IMF reports from 1975. That seems to have been the
focus of economic debate in the House, but actually I could not find any. Instead, I went
to the 2008 IMF report, where the IMF ta lked about a number of issues facing New
Zealand, including what it described in careful bureaucratic language as “rapidly
appreciating house prices”. It noted that in response to rising inflation the official cash
rate reached 8.25 percent and homeowners faced floating mortgage rates of 11 percent.
The current account deficit was 8 percent. All of those numbers are about double what
they are now, and they are measures of the wreckage that the previous Labour
Government did to the New Zealand economy.

State-owned Assets, Sales—Progress, Ownership of Genesis Energy Shares, and
Purpose
3. Hon TAU HENARE (National) to the Minister of Finance: What progress is the
Government making with its share offer programm e to free up capital to invest in new
public assets without having to borrow more from overseas lenders?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Government is making very
good progress. L ast month the Government confirmed that Genesis Energy shares had
been priced at $1.55 in the share offer book build, which was the first stage of the offer.
The general offer opened on 29 March and closes tomorrow. The total proceeds from
the share offer will be up to $726 million, with $620 million already committed through
the book build, so we will hand $726 million of share certificates to investors and they
will hand us $726 million in cash. That means that the Government will raise $4.7
billion on behalf of taxpayers from the four share offers. That means we will be able to
use that money to build hospitals, build schools, maintain KiwiRail, and roll out ultra -
fast broadband without having to go and borrow from the Opposition’s obvious friends,
the overseas bankers.

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: What percentage of Genesis Energy shares is expected to be held
by New Zealanders after the share offer is completed?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Right at the start of the programme, the Government se t a
target of 85 percent New Zealand ownership. I know that many people were sceptical at
that time that 85 percent New Zealand ownership could be achieved. In the case of
Genesis Energy, it is expected that around 88 percent of Genesis Energy will be owne d
by New Zealanders at the completion of the share offer, so Kiwi investors have been at
the front of the queue for shares. What that demonstrates is that New Zealanders are
quite capable of making their own decisions, without having to rely on the Governm ent,
about investing their savings in large, successful New Zealand companies. Quite why
anyone would want to take that opportunity away from them is hard to understand.

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: How many of the objectives that the Government set for  the
Genesis Energy share offer and the wider share offer programme have been met?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Despite the best efforts of the Opposition and the Māori
Council, we have achieved all of the objectives that we set. I am pleased to report that
the four objectives were 51 percent Government ownership, which has been achieved;
New Zealanders at the fro nt of the queue, which has been achieved; companies that
provide good opportunities for investors, which has been achieved; and the freed -up
capital being spent on new public assets, which has certainly been achieved. The
Government is satisfied that indus try-specific regulation continues to protect New
Zealand consumers who, in the long run, are the ultimate beneficiaries of this
programme.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: And what about the money? Has his objective regarding how
much he was going to raise been achieved; if not, what is the difference? [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I particularly want to hear the answer.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes. We set the —[Interruption] Well, a far -sighted
Government back in 2011 set a range of $5 billion to $7 billion in a programme that
included Solid Energy. Solid Energy has dropped out, and so with one less company we
almost got to $5 billion —$4.7 billion. But I can assure the Opposition that that is
enough money to buy some things and build some public assets in election year.

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: What new public assets will the Government buy using proceeds
from the share offer programme?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, it is a very, very long list, but I will limit myself to just
a few. The Government has so far allocated just $2 billion of the $4.7 billion. This
includes $426 million for redeveloping the Christchurch hospitals, one of the largest
17174 Questions for Oral Answer 10 Apr 2014
single public construction projects for a long time; $50 million to speed up the School
Network Upgrade Project, so our children can have access to the best technology; $94
million for the fourth year of KiwiRail’s Turnaround Plan; and a substantial
contribution to building the new schools in Christchurch.
Transport Infrastructure—Napier-Gisborne Freight
4. DENIS O’ROURKE (NZ First)  to the Minister of Transport : Does he agree
with the conclusion in the 2012 New Zealand Transport Agency commissioned report
by Opus International that coastal shipping, followed by rail, are the most cost effective
modes of transporting freight over long distances in New Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: The statement included in
that question comes from a very simplistic reading of that report, as it depends on which
item is being freighted at any one time. What that report did was take one container and
send it on five different modes around New Zea land, and it concluded that that was an
exhaustive way of working out what was the best way to transport any goods around
this country. So I do not agree with the statement in its entirety.
Denis O’Rourke : Why has he rejected the Hawke’s B ay Regional Council’s
initiative to invest $5.5 million of ratepayers’ money over 5 years to re -establish a rail
service on the mothballed Napier -Gisborne line if the Government makes a similar
modest investment of $3 million to $4 million in repairs to th e damaged track and other
infrastructure, so that a locally established company can lease the restored line and
purchase the rolling stock from KiwiRail?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Because I have great respect for the ratepayers of that
district. Secondly, what I would tell the member is that if you look at the freight demand
coming out of the area right now, for 2 months of the year it puts an extra 17 trucks on
the road per day, and that is all that is in the increase. We have looked at that proposal.
It comes from a group of people who are very keen on the idea, but it simply does not
stack up. If we supported it, it would be a tragedy for the New Zealand taxpayer, and it
would be a bigger tragedy for the ratepayers of the Hawke’s Bay.
Denis O’Rourke : Is the Minister aware that the council and the Napier Gisborne
Rail Establishment Group consider that his ill -considered rejection of the initiative is
based on a significant misunderstanding of their proposal; if so, will he now  reconsider
it in the comprehensive manner that it actually deserves?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: We have considered that proposal in a very
comprehensive way. What I would say to the member is that if the Hawke’s Bay people
are so keen on fund ing that rail line, why do they need the relatively modest part from
the Government, as he suggests? If it is so good and it is going to work so well, why do
they not just come along and say: “Let us have the track, so that we can make it all
work.”?
Denis O’Rourke: Does the Minister accept that this region cannot depend solely on
a narrow winding State highway when the log harvest alone heading for the Port of
Napier is expected to go from 90,000 tonnes per annum at present to around 900,0 00
tonnes within a few years, adding at least 180 more logging truck movements 6 days a
week on a road that is already congested with heavy vehicles; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: It will not matter how emphatic the member is in
asking a question loaded with bogus facts. The reality is that no logs have travelled on
that line at any point. Secondly, the so -called wall of wood has been promised for
decades. Thirdly, until it does materialise, until it is there, why on earth would y ou
expect the Government to put the head of the ratepayers in that district in the noose for
some people who, in the end, will not accept that their figures are not good enough to
make it work?

Denis O’Rourke: Does the Minister confirm tha t the creation recently of nine new
passing areas on State Highway 2 between Napier and Gisborne at a cost of $4 million,
made possible by a special Crown contribution and the National Land Transport
Programme allocation of $9 million to $10 million over a  3-year period to improve the
condition of that highway for a large increase in truck movements, means that the
Government will continue to favour expensive but relatively minor road improvements
over a rail restoration proposal with a much better cost -benefit ratio in both the short
and long terms?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: If this member keeps on putting these figures in front
of us, David Cunliffe is going to reconsider his coalition options. There is no way that
anything he has said makes any sense. Yes, we put more money into making that road
safer, because, surprisingly, 97 percent of all the freight coming out of that area has
always gone on the road.
Denis O’Rourke: Are there any plans to extend electrification of the r ail network,
and, in doing so, retain the valuable human resource of the expert and skilled team that
is undertaking the Auckland rail network electrification; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Certainly not on the Gisborne to Napier line.
Denis O’Rourke: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: This is a point of order, and I want to hear it in silence.
Denis O’Rourke: The question had nothing to do with the Napier-Gisborne line, and
was a general question—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am going to, on this occasion, ask the member to repeat the
question.
Denis O’Rourke: The question was this: are there any plans to extend electrification
of the rail network, and, in doing so, retain the valuable human resource of the expert
and skilled team that is undertaking the Auckland rail network electrification; if not,
why not?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Not at this point.
District Health Boards—Resourcing and Service Delivery
5. Hon ANNETTE KING (Labour —Rongotai) to the Minister of Health : What
recent reports has he seen on the funding of hospitals in New Zealand ?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: I have seen reports that show that
despite tight financial times this Government has increased funding for health by an
average of $500 million a year and that health will ag ain be the top priority for more
investment in the upcoming Budget. I have also seen a report that showed that despite
nearly doubling the health budget more people thought the health system had got worse.

items.speaker: The report noted
items.text: “It is inconceivable that a Gove rnment could spend so much money
and make the system worse.” Of course, this report was from the Dominion Post  in
2007 and referred to the previous Labour Government.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: Who was the Minister?

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Not me. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! If some members want to get away early to clean up for the
reception tonight, they may well get the chance.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Oh, no Mr Speaker, I am enjoying it. Will he dismi ss the
concerns of the representative of senior doctors in our hospitals who said last week that
staff shortages and underfunding are putting hospitals under intense pressure, and we
now have a health system that is prone to “erratic decision -making, heavy -handed
management, and gaga behaviour”; if so, why?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: Of course I would completely reject that assessment from the
union. That union increasingly looks like a branch of the Labour Party, and that
statement certainly confirms it.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: With district health boards like Waikato having 61 nursing
vacancies and 18 senior doctor vacancies, and the Southern District Health Board
having 58 nursing vacancies and 12 senior doctor vacancies, leading to sta ffing
shortages and pressure on existing staff, should staff publicly state their concern and
distress over unsafe working conditions and stressful staff levels, or are they just being
union activists?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: I think it is perfectly legitimate for staff to use the appropriate
processes if they have any concern in respect of patient safety. What I would have to
say is that if it is correct that there are 61 nurse vacancies in the Waikato, it would be
nice if the member also said that  there are actually 2,000 nurses employed by the
Waikato District Health Board, and that 61 certainly sounds more like 3 percent, which
is nowhere near the big shock, horror story that that member would like to portray.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Is he aware that there has been in increase of 18 percent in older
New Zealanders turning up to emergency departments over the last 4 years, and that this
is now leading to huge staff pressure, staff burnout, low staff morale, and concern at
patient safety; if so, is this just union members talking?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: Quite the opposite. I think the health service is providing
better care for older people when they present to the emergency department. It is faster
and better than it has ever be en, and quite different from when that member was a
Minister in a Government where old people languished on trolleys in corridors under
bright fluorescent lights for days on end.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Is he aware that some district health bo ards are now
implementing service reductions, driven by budgetary constraints—particularly in home
care—so they can meet the pressure in hospitals, for example, in the Capital and Coast
District Health Board where Official Information Act information shows  that on
average there has been a 37 percent reduction of service to people requiring home care
over the last 3 years?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: More money than ever is being invested in home -care
services right across New Zealand. The Government has  more money put in there. I
think last year’s Budget put more money into home -care services as well. There has
been a very significant investment.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I am sure you heard my
question—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I did hear your question.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: —and it was not about—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I heard the question. I now have to decide. The question
effectively was: “Is he aware of increasing pressure on home care because of financial
pressure?”. The Minister answered that by saying there was more money being debated.
The question has been addressed. If the member has a further supplementary we will
listen to it.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: No, but I’d like one.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER

Methamphetamine Action Plan—Initiatives and Funding
6. MIKE SABIN (National —Northland) to the Minister of Police : What steps is
the Government taking to reduce the supply of methamphetamine and its precursors into
New Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: This week the Minister of Customs and
I announced $1.1 million will be used to place a police attaché officer in Guangdong

with Chinese enforcement agencies. This police officer will help to identify organised
criminals attempting to smug gle methamphetamine and its precursors into New
Zealand. This funding will also be used for Customs Service and police staff to take part

precursors and smuggle them into New Ze aland, and this programme is expected to

Methamphetamine Action Plan. When this plan was established in 2009 the
Government committed to using the money recovered from criminals to target the drug
trade and help thos e affected by it to get treatment. In other words, the criminals are
paying us to catch them and treat their victims. It is a nice irony. Since the Criminal
Proceeds (Recovery) Act came into force, $39.4 million has been forfeited to the
Crown, over half o f which has come from methamphetamine -associated offences.

increase in residential alcohol and drug treatment, enhanced front -line screening at the

VETERANS’ SUPPORT BILL
Second Reading

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: I move, That the
Veterans’ Support Bill be now read a second time . On behalf of the Minister of
Veterans’ Affairs, Michael Woodhouse, I would , firstly, like to th ank the Social
Services Committee for its hard work in examining the bill. It has carefully reviewed
the bill to ensure that it is a fitting replacement and provides adequate support for not
only our current veterans but also our future veterans. Service i n defence of our nation
and for freedom and democracy around the world is a sacrifice that needs appropriate
recognition in legislation. I would also like to thank veterans for their feedback on the
bill.
The bill received a number of submissions, which w ere carefully considered by the
committee. Although submitters focused on various issues, responses indicated an
underlying support for the new legislation. [Interruption]

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Would members
leaving the Chamber please show some respect to the member trying to address the
House.

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: It was also important to get feedback from the veterans
affected by this legislation, and the submissions received showed, for the main part, that
we have drafted legislation that meets veterans’ needs.
The bill replaces the War Pensions Act 1954 and originates from the 2010 report of
the Law Commission that followed an extensive review of the wa r pensions scheme.
The 1954 Act was found by the Law Commission to be outdated, unwieldy, and no
longer fitting the needs of the veterans it was intended to support. The Law Commission
made a large number of recommendations, the vast majority of which were  accepted by
this Government. The bill continues and enhances the previous entitlements under the
old Act and it retains the key principles of benevolence. Service eligibility criteria will
remain the same, and all deployments currently covered will be cov ered under the new
legislation.
The bill contains two schemes and it introduces several new entitlements. Scheme
one will cover veterans who served from the Second World War through to, and
including, the Viet Nam War. Their entitlements will continue to be based on those
available under the 1954 Act. Scheme two will cover those who served in a recognised
war or in emergencies since 1 April 1974. The entitlements will be closely aligned with
those available under ACC, but with an additional top -up that rec ognises the special
nature of military service. The bill will also include a more modernised approach to
rehabilitation. Submissions confirmed general support for these proposals. In addition,
submitters recommended changes to some key areas. It is pleasin g to see that, where
appropriate, the committee has recommended that changes be made to the bill to reflect
these.
One of the key changes made by the committee is to the threshold for the veterans
pension. Submissions questioned whether 55 percent was the  appropriate level of
whole-person impairment to use as a threshold for the veterans pension and other
entitlements, noting that it did not appear to be the equivalent of the threshold currently
used in the 1954 Act. The information that was provided to th e committee established
that 52 percent whole -person impairment was, in fact, the most equivalent threshold,
and in order to not disadvantage veterans, the threshold will be moved from 55 percent
to 52 percent. To further ensure that no veterans are disadvantaged by this provision, the
17188 Veterans’ Support Bill 10 Apr 2014
bill has been amended to provide that a veteran or other claimant who currently meets
the threshold for entitlement under the 1954 Act will continue to do so if they claim
under this bill.
I note that a minority on the commi ttee suggested that the disablement threshold for
veterans pension eligibility should change from 54 percent on the new scale all the way
to zero. In 2012 the Government announced a new $60 million package over 5 years to
improve the support and recognitio n given to veterans who have served New Zealand,
and it agreed to adopt in full or in part 132 of the Law Commission’s 170 uncosted
recommendations. The decision was made by Cabinet at the time not to discard the
impairment threshold for veterans pension, but to retain the status quo.
The war disablement pension and veterans pension represent forms of compensation
from the Government for those who have suffered injury or impairment as a result of
their military service and for their families. Removing a le vel of disablement as a
requirement in order to receive a veterans pension and access its associated benefits
would be a significant departure from the current rationale, which has existed since the
veterans pension was first introduced. It would cost more  than $40 million over the first
4 years alone, with most of this cost coming directly from the lump -sum payment that is
triggered by the death of a veteran. This bill is about supporting our veterans. Removing
the disablement threshold would have a signif icant cost, but would do little to increase
the support offered to veterans during their lifetime. As it fundamentally changes the
rationale behind the veterans pension and does not represent well -targeted spending, we
do not support this move.
Another ar ea of change is to the decision -making provisions and the points of
reference for deciding claims. Underlying the rewrite of the 1954 Act was a desire not
only to modernise the legislation but to make it more accessible for both veterans and
administrators to understand and use. The evidential provisions underlying eligibility
for entitlements in the bill are fundamental, and they received scrutiny in many of the
public submissions. There was very broad support for the use of the Australian
statements of principle as the main reference point for deciding claims. The statements
of principle are comprehensive, soundly based in medical terms, and introduce a much -
needed element of certainty to the process.
The bill also needed to modernise the legal and eviden tial tests for establishing
entitlement, and these were the subject of many submissions. It became clear that more
work was needed to reduce legal jargon and ensure that the provisions are clearer, easier
to understand, and fully aligned with the benevolen ce principle in decision making. The
committee made several changes to the bill as a result of these submissions. As a result,
I am confident that the decision -making and legal provisions of the bill will serve the
decision-making process well in the futur e. In summary, the Government is committed
to improving veterans’ support, and this is reflected in this very important bill, as
reported back by the committee. I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: Just before I start on this Veterans’
Support Bill, I acknowledge the work of a senior researcher for Labour, Bridget Service,
who helped on this bill and who is leaving after many years of hard work on behalf of
our MPs here. Thank you, Bridget, for the work that you have done on our behalf.
I want to come now to the bill and say that I respond with amazement to Nathan
Guy’s statement that it was important to get feedback from the veterans and to meet the
veterans’ needs. We  sat through those submissions and we heard —unlike the Acting
Minister—what the veterans said and what the Royal New Zealand Returned and
Services Association said about the inadequacy of some parts of this bill.
I reject the Minister’s statement that ther e are no grounds for removing the
requirement that before a person is eligible for a veterans pension they have to be
10 Apr 2014 Veterans’ Support Bill 17189
significantly disabled. What the RSA told the Social Services Committee, and what the
veterans have told the select committee, and what Ne w Zealanders would support is
this: if you are a New Zealander eligible for New Zealand superannuation and you have
served your country in an overseas deployment gazetted by the Minister and recognised
by the Chief of Defence Force as having put yourself i n harm’s way, then surely that is
the appropriate threshold for a person to be eligible for a veterans pension. That was
recommended by the Law Commission. That was asked for by the New Zealand RSA.
That is what the families of the veterans who sacrificed so much thought was
appropriate and the National Government ignored those views, those requests, and those
pleadings.
I have here a letter from the RSA. It is signed by the national president Lieutenant
General Don McIver, a man who is much respected in t his House. He said that it was
very disappointing that the Social Services Committee decided not to progress the
removal of the requirement of serious impairment before you are eligible for a veterans
pension. He said it is particularly disappointing to th ose veterans who have served their
country with loyalty and with honour but it is also disappointing to the RSA
membership as a whole.
He raises the question in this letter —and it has gone to various members of this
House—that during the Law Commission’s processes and the Law Commission review
that led to this legislation, the commission strongly recommended that the threshold of
serious impairment be removed. He said: “Neither we nor the commission were able to
find out why it should be necessary to be si gnificantly disabled to qualify for the
veterans pension.” He says that the 52 percent significant disability figure is entirely
arbitrary. He asked officials time and again at the select committee what the grounds
were for saying that before a person can get a veterans pension, they must have 52
percent of total disability. No answer was given except that that was historically the
case. There was no rationale; it was entirely arbitrary.
The other thing the RSA points out is something that I concur with str ongly. It points
out that although the Government gave no explanation for its decision, it declined the
submission, saying: “Not progressed at this point of time.” Not progressed at this point
of time. We are talking about 16,700 elderly veterans, many of whom left their families
and served this country for years overseas, putting themselves at harm’s risk, and who
are dying in their droves at the moment because they are in their 80s and 90s. “Not
progressed at this point of time.” is a cynical answer from a Government that knows
time is not on the side of our veterans.
We are not asking for a lot. Nobody gets the veterans pension, first of all, until they
have reached the age of superannuation. That is 65 at the present time. You do not get
the veterans pension on top of superannuation; you get it instead of superannuation. So
the costs are actually quite small. The relatively small benefits are a gesture of gratitude
by us to those who put their lives in the firing line on behalf of their country. It is ab out
getting a community services card. It is about, if you are in hospital for more than 13
weeks, being able to retain your pension rather than losing it, and it is about a lump sum
payment on death. Yes, the Minister is right. That lump sum payment will usually go to
the widow. But surely the widow is entitled to something in recognition of what she
gave up while her husband or partner was serving this country for long years during the
Second World War.
This year, 2014, is a special year. It is a special  year because we commemorate the
centenary of 100,000 New Zealanders going to serve in the First World War of whom
one in five died and six out of 10 were either killed or injured. Twenty years later our
parents’ generation went to serve in th e Second Worl d W ar and another 12,000 lost
their lives. The people came back after years of serving their country and many of them
17190 Veterans’ Support Bill 10 Apr 2014
were scarred inside and often scarred physically as well. Why is it so much to ask this
Government that instead of just rhetoric about our  gratitude to the veterans we actually
give them something tangible? There are 16,700 of them at the moment and do you
know what it is going to cost? I asked Veterans Affairs, so I have the official figures. In
the first year it will cost $11.1 million. Th at is 2014 -15. By 2017 -18, in 3 years’ time,
that will be down to $8 million—just $8 million—because of the level of the passing on
of the World War II and the Korean War veterans.
What I am saying —and I have been totally upfront in the select committee, as
members will attest, and to the Minister—is that there is a gap in this bill. There is a gap
that the Law Commission, which did all of the hard yards on this bill, recommended
should be closed. There is a gap in this bill, which the RSA with its wisdom and its right
to represent the interests of veterans, said “Please fix this.” The Government has not,
because it says that it will cost too much. On one hand, there will be $60 million spent
over 5 years. On the other hand, just $11 million dropping to $8 million a year is
required to fill that gap to enable the people who have returned as veterans to have the
pride of saying: “I am not just a superannuitant; I am a war veteran.” That is what they
want it for. They are not actually even particularly interes ted in these small financial
benefits. They want to have the pride of saying: “I have served my country.” What
better way of saying that than to say: “I am in receipt of a veterans pension. This is how
my country has recognised what I have done on behalf o f my nation.” That is what we
are asking for.
In the Committee of the whole House, I will be moving an amendment through a
Supplementary Order Paper to pick up the Law Commission’s recommendation, to pick
up what those veterans have asked us so sincerely for, and to pick up what the RSA says
is a major gap in this legislation.
I have one other comment, and it is to the Minister of Defence. We know that morale
and attrition rates have reached a record low in the case of morale and a record high in
the case of attrition. We know that when the Auditor -General reported on this she said
that is because this Government is perceived by the men and women of the New
Zealand Defence Force to have broken the social contract between Government and the
services. They have no union and they cannot negotiate their conditions.
I want to say to the Minister of Defence —and I say it sincerely —that the best way
we can tell our current serving members of the New Zealand Defence Force that we
honour their commitment and service  is to pass something that recognises that we see
our commitment extending into their retirement years. The best way we can deal with
the problems of recruitment and retention is to send that message to our serving soldiers
today. It will not cost us much for another 30 years. Most of those who have served in
Timor-Leste, the Solomons, Afghanistan, and Bosnia will not be retiring for 30 years.
But this year —the centenary of our joining the First World War —is surely the
appropriate time to say to our vetera ns that we honour them not simply with our
rhetoric, but that we honour them with a practical measure that they have asked for and
we can easily deliver, and that is affordable and justified. I commend my
Supplementary Order Paper to the House in the Committee of the whole House.

items.speaker: MELISSA LEE
items.text: Ahn yung ha se yo. It is a great pleasure to rise to
support the second reading of the Veterans’ Support Bill. Before I get on with my
contribution, I would just like to make a comment. It is lovely to see the passion in Mr
Goff’s speech. We have seen that in the Social Services Committee and in the House. I
just wish he had been as passionate when he was responsible for the Treasury benches
when Labour was in the position of Government —in the 9 years that it was in
Government. Now that he is in Opposition, he basically says passionately: “Why does
this National Government not do something about it?”. He had the opportunity; he was
10 Apr 2014 Veterans’ Support Bill 17191
actually the Minister of Defence. He could have really done something about it, but he
did not. Now that he is in Opposition, he can throw stones.
The men and women who serve in our defence forces, now and in the past, for
freedom and democracy need to be recognised for the sacrifices tha t they have made. I
am a recipient of those sacrifices. Having met lots of Korean veterans who have come
back from the war —there were people who were injured, and there were people who
died during the Korean War —and, being born in Korea, I grew up with the  knowledge
that we must be grateful for the ultimate sacrifices of the veterans who actually paid
with their lives in a war that divided my birth country. We owe a great debt to our
veterans, and this National-led Government is committed to honouring their service, and
better meeting the needs of older veterans who need help to maintain their homes and of
veterans of modern-day deployments.
This bill has many of the same provisions as the current Act. The criteria for service
eligibility will stay the same , as will health care treatment. Accepted conditions will
continue to be funded. No veteran will have their entitlements reduced; in fact,
thousands will benefit from increased care and support. That has to be better. It has been
quite a process to rewrite  a 60-year-old Act, an Act that was designed to deal with the
physical risk associated with deployment but did not actually cover the psychological
and environmental risks that veterans have faced. The Law Commission’s findings after
reviewing the Act stat ed that the Act was outdated and unwieldy, and no longer fitted
the needs of the veterans it served. This Veterans’ Support Bill actually fixes that.
There are two schemes. Scheme One comes into force on 1 July this year, and runs
until 1 July 2015 to cover all veterans as a transitional measure. After that, Scheme One
will apply to veterans with service from World War II to the Viet Nam War. The
entitlements will be based on what is already available, with some improvements such
as when a veteran is under  the age of retirement and unable work they will receive a
higher rate of income compensation than is now available. The rate paid will be based
on 80 percent of the average wage, an increase of about $200 gross for most of the
recipients. Scheme Two cover s veterans with service since 1974, when ACC was
introduced, and comes into force on July 1 next year. In 2015 there will also be changes
to the eligibility criteria for accessing support services such as home help and
lawnmowing.
This is a bill that the select committee considered very carefully. I do understand the
passion behind Mr Goff’s speech, and most of us in some way understand where that
passion comes from, because we do all support the veterans who have paid greatly
through their service in serv ice of their country and people. We appreciate their
participation in battles overseas, with the New Zealand flag on their chests, serving our
nation proudly. This is a great improvement on the 1954 Act, which is totally outdated.
It is a great improvement , and I believe it is something that the veterans have been
waiting for. Thank you.
