An amount of $11 million cannot be money the Government cannot find. The
Government found a billion dollars to give tax cuts to the top 10 percent. It found $800
million to bail out South Canterbury Finance. It found $30 million to bail out Rio Tinto.
It found $27 million to give to private schools. The money is out there. The Government
is perfectly capable of spending money on the people whom it chooses. Why cannot it
spend this tiny amount of money on veterans? Why? I want to hear from the members
opposite as to why that is. Why is it that the Government cannot spend that money?
As I said, though, that is a change to the legislation  that we do want to see, but
overall this is an improvement on what we had before, because the 1954 legislation was
becoming outdated and it was becoming outmoded. That is why Labour initi ated the
review of the legislation. The 1954 Act actually had not changed in any significant way
in the —I am trying to count —many, many decades since it was first enacted. As is
often the case, it was legislation that was responsive to the needs at the tim e and it was
responsive primarily to the needs of World War II veterans. Of course, it came in about
two decades before ACC was established. ACC has changed the playing field for what
veterans are entitled to and what they can receive through the normal so cial security
framework that we have in New Zealand. So we needed a new system that not only
recognised the change but recognised that we have some veterans who receive an
entitlement based on the service that they gave before ACC came in and other veteran s
on the service that they undertook after ACC came in. So the bill acknowledges those
differences and sets up two separate schemes for those different groups of veterans, and
that is a significant improvement.
Overall, what this legislation does is it implements a number of the Law Commission
recommendations. We think it should implement more of them and we have a
Supplementary Order Paper to that effect, but in general we do support this legislation.

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker. I am pleased to rise and
take a call on, and offer the Green Party’s support for, the second reading of the
Veterans’ Support Bill. I am not, however, as pleased as I would have liked to be, as not
all the issues that we ha d hoped to see resolved within the Social Services Committee
have been resolved. But, clearly, the 40,000 veterans with qualifying service and their
families have been waiting 7 years since this issue was first referred to the Law
Commission and, you know, it seems about time. The 1954 Act clearly needs updating.
So for those reasons we are absolutely supporting this bill today. It is time for some
resolution. It is time for families to be able to move forward.
The Law Commission made 170 recommendations f or updating the Act. The
Government has accepted 132 of those recommendations, and during the select
committee process we heard very well -informed submissions from many presenters on
issues of a technical as well as a more fundamental nature. The basic shi ft of this bill is
that it will make changes to the administration and decision -making processes, provide
a greater focus on rehabilitation, and enable the provision of services to better meet the
needs of elderly veterans as well as those of modern-day and future deployments.
Changes have been made through the select committee, and I would like to
acknowledge the committee and the presenters for the process that has brought this bill
17194 Veterans’ Support Bill 10 Apr 2014
back to the House, even with our reservations. I do believe that we all want a system
that appropriately acknowledges those whom this country has sent to war. I share, I
guess, the slight bemusement from Labour colleagues about not understanding really
why the threshold was not taken out of this bill, and I have not heard from  the
Government a reason that makes sense to me on that.
I am a pacifist and the Green Party is founded on a principle of non -violence. After
watching the incredibly moving film last night Field Punishment No. 1 , I cannot help
but reflect on the pointlessness and brutality of many, if not all, wars and reflect on how
much better it would be if no person ever picked up arms. The film, which I really think
everyone should watch, showed how during the First World War conscientious
objectors from New Zealand were sent to the Western Front and tortured for refusing to
become soldiers. It also highlighted the brutality of war and reminded me that soldiers
are real people, members of our communities and our families, as well as being
members of our armed forces.
The images we saw last night reminded me of the stories we heard from submitters
who have been in our armed forces and told us of lives irrevocably changed by war,
and, in the case of the children, how the parents’ experience was at times passed on to
the children. When the parents did not get the rehabilitation or psychological assistance
they needed, the damage that was caused to those parents through that experience of
war was at times passed on to their children as their homes became war zones as they
lived out that post-traumatic stress in the home.
We also heard of years of battles to get help and of struggles for recognition —battles
and struggles with the same State that sent these people into places that caused them
harm. You do not have to believe in war to want the best support for people who have
been through such horror, which is why the main point of contention I have with this
bill as it is being reported back is that it does not go far enough.
The bill does not pick up the Law Commission reco mmendation and the
recommendation of many submitters, including the Royal New Zealand Returned and
Services’ Association, that all veterans with qualifying service should be eligible for the
veterans pension. It seems to me that that policy would have had several advantages. It
would have simplified our system and removed some of what we believe is unnecessary
conflict that exists within the system as it is at the moment. Although that might sound
like that is triggering dollar signs for people, as has alre ady been noted by the Hon Phil
Goff, the cost of that in the first year would be $11 million and the cost is projected to
decrease to $8 million in the year after. That does not seem like an insurmountable,
unbearable cost for this country to bear. If the fear is possible costs as a result of more
conflicts in the future, well, we would hope that this would be another thing to consider
before entering into a conflict. If we cannot afford to recognise people for the cost of
going into those wars, then we really do need to second-guess our decisions to go.
The primary advantage, as we see it, would be that it would acknowledge the debt of
the State to our veterans. Most people serving in the armed services are not there to go
to war; they are there for many o ther reasons. If the State does send them to war, I
believe a debt is owed, regardless of the degree of injury.
The second point that we are unresolved over is the portability point. Again, this
elicited a large number of submissions asking this House to uncouple the portability
arrangements for the veterans pension from superannuation rules. It was submitted that
the veterans pension is earned in recognition of a duty to the Crown by way of military
service putting veterans in harm’s way, and not by livin g in New Zealand for a specific
period of time. Again, the Royal New Zealand Returned and Services’ Association
expressed concerns that there were many New Zealand military veterans —particularly
10 Apr 2014 Veterans’ Support Bill 17195
Pacific Islanders—who were otherwise entitled at age 65 but w ho did not qualify due to
residency requirements.
The counter view to this was that the majority of veterans living overseas reside in
countries with which New Zealand has a social security arrangement, and therefore they
are able to access the pension. O f course, of those in places without an agreement, the
majority at the moment live in the Cook Islands. New Zealand has just announced a
change to this arrangement so that veterans wishing to retire in the Cook Islands, Niue,
and Tokelau will be covered.
The Law Commission also noted in its review that the major concern regarding
portability was for those under superannuation age. This bill resolves that issue by
instating a veterans’ weekly income compensation that does not have a residence
criteria. With  that all said, we still retain concerns about any future conflicts and
entitlement for people who wish to retire in other Pacific Islands —for example, Tonga
or Samoa. We believe the principle —and possibly, more importantly, the symbolism —
of entitlement holds a meaning beyond the financial benefits of the pension.
We would have preferred to uncouple the pension from superannuation to ensure all
qualifying veterans were entitled regardless of where they live. These two points are
really our only sticking points with this bill. Again, we want to acknowledge the need to
update the War Pensions Act and improve the processes for veterans.
War and armed conflict are a horror and a failure of humanity that we should do
everything in our power to avoid. When the S tate fails to avoid war, the State has a
particular responsibility for those who pay the price of that failure with their health and
their freedom. With respect to the human frailty of those who end up fighting the wars
created by political leaders —and in the knowledge that this bill will not in any way
make going to war more attractive —we wholeheartedly support this bill as the least our
country can do to acknowledge the cost of being asked to kill another and putting your
life and body on the line. We commend it to the House.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: I would like to add my words to that and concur
with my parliamentary colleague in regard to the fact that war and conflict are
unnecessary evils. But there are t imes when people lose sight of the humanity, and,
therefore, we are faced with the reality that in order to keep peace and harmony in
existence, there are drastic measures that have to be taken. So we end up in this place. I
think it is not the place, real ly, or appropriate for us, in this place and in this time, to
argue about who did what and who did not do what. In order to honour the memory and
to honour the aspect of the support that we need and want to give to our veterans, it is
important to be able to progress this through to a place in which they receive the support
that they so desperately need.
Can I also acknowledge Major Rebecca Thornley, who is in the gallery and who led
the work with the rest of the Defence Force and Veteran Affairs. It was w ork that I
know must have been very difficult, not only to hear the stories but also the role that
they had to play, knowing the legacy that has gone before them and what they needed to
do in order to ensure that the future of other veterans will be served  by this. So can I
acknowledge you and honour you for the work that you have done. It is not an easy
place to be.
This bill, the Veterans’ Support Bill, has come about through the Law Commission.
In 2007 that review was initiated. This bill replaces an Ac t that is nearly 60 years old.
As was just said, out of the 170 recommendations, 132 were implemented. Therefore, it
is important to note that in the implementation of that review there were some things,
obviously, that were not able to get through. But we  can have some confidence—hence
the reason why we have support across the House —that we have worked diligently and
effectively to ensure that we have heard the submissions and worked with officials to
17196 Veterans’ Support Bill 10 Apr 2014
ensure that we have a bill that will definitely meet th e core issues of importance for our
veterans in particular.
The Veterans’ Support Bill is now all -encompassing. That ensures that it actually
meets the needs of veterans and provides for treatment and rehabilitation for accepted
conditions. One of the cha llenges is that in the previous Act, the War Pensions Act
1954—and I think this is an important part —I know, for many of us, it was often silent
on the provision of rehabilitation, and the compensation was often focused on physical
disability without ackno wledging the emotional or mental effects and the need for
rehabilitation in those areas as well. So I believe that this has been important, as it has
actually answered some of the concerns that were put forward in the submissions as
well.
Just a couple of other important points. I think there was concern raised about the
importance of support for surviving spouses of veterans. As part of this package we
have also increased the war disablement pension and the surviving spouse pension by 5
percent last year, on top of inflation. We think that is important as well.
More than 20,000 modern defence force personnel are now veterans, and there is a
need to have a legislative framework that supports all our veterans. It is never going to
be the perfect bill, but it  is the right bill. It strikes the right balance, to make sure that it
actually meets the needs of our war veterans. Along with others, I do support this bill. It
is the centennial next year, 2015, to commemorate 100 years of the New Zealand
Defence Force.  Along with Poto Williams I have also been working with the Cook
Islands community to ensure that we remember all of those, right throughout our
communities, who have served and sacrificed themselves for New Zealand. We have
put this bill forward with the recommendation that it will truly support and meet their
needs as well. I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: I rise on behalf of New Zealand First to speak
on the Veterans’ Suppo rt Bill. Around this Chamber, on the various crests and plaques,
are the names of many of the great battles and campaigns that New Zealand has
participated in. When you look around this Chamber and you see names such as Monte
Cassino, Korea, Passchendaele,  Viet Nam, Malaysia, and all the others around these
walls, it is a solemn reminder to us all as members of Parliament of the huge
commitment that our men and women have made in the service of this country in so
many campaigns abroad. That service was usua lly undertaken to uphold democracy and
to ensure that others living in other parts of the world can hopefully enjoy the same
quality of life that we enjoy here in New Zealand.
The men and women who have gone abroad have put their lives at risk. They have
done that voluntarily. They have not had to go abroad; they did not have to join the
services in many instances, apart from, of course, earlier, in World War I or World War
II, when they were called up. But many in recent campaigns have done this as
volunteers in the services, including in the instance of the Viet Nam War, where my
brother was killed. All those who went to Viet Nam volunteered to go as Regular Force
soldiers. They did not have to go but they volunteered to be part of it. Many of those
servicemen and servicewomen from the likes of the Korean campaign, Viet Nam, and,
indeed, some from World War II as well —who are now getting very elderly —deserve
the absolute respect that this House should give and that the Parliament of this country
should give. They should be given all that is due to them.
In 2007 the Law Commission put forward 170 recommendations to this House. One
hundred and thirty -two have been picked up by the Government to go forward; the
remainder have not. In particular, the area the Government has not picked up is where
the Law Commission recommended that if you have served abroad on behalf of this
country, you should be entitled at age 65, when you are eligible to receive
10 Apr 2014 Veterans’ Support Bill 17197
superannuation, to receive a war veterans pension. That would then recognise that any
person retiring who has served this country abroad has put themselves on the line and
that they have come back. It would recognise the fact that they are not just a
superannuitant but they are a superannuitant who has served this country.
The small amount of additional money to provide those superannuitants with a war
pension, to provide them with an automatic community services card, to ensure that
they retain their pension after being in hospital for more than 13 weeks, and to give their
spouse or family a lump sum on death is such a small amount as recognition of, and
compensation for, having served their country. I am absolutely appalled, having lost
somebody in Viet Nam, having lost uncles in World War II, and having lost relati ves in
World War I as well, that this Government cannot see fit to find $11.1 million —$11.1
million—in 2014 -15 to ensure that those veterans are properly recognised in this
manner.
We have put forward a minority report, as has the Labour Party —and the Lab our
Party one is supported by the Green Party—and in it we have stated “New Zealand First
is firmly of the view that the Veterans’ Support Bill is long overdue. The Law
Commission first reported in 2010 and four years later this legislation is finally reaching
its conclusion. Progress should have been made with much greater urgency. A great
many veterans are affected by this review. They are not getting any younger.”—they are
not getting any younger. “They deserve far greater respect for the service they ha ve
given to their country. Expediency in completing this exercise would be in order.”

items.speaker: The report further states
items.text: “The National Government has rejected the Law
Commission’s recommendation that all veterans who have served on an overseas
operational deployme nt for the New Zealand Defence Force should be eligible for a
veterans’ pension if they meet the criteria for New Zealand Superannuation. New
Zealand First supports the recommendations of the New Zealand Law Commission to
lower the entitlement threshold to  zero percent, which is strongly supported by the
Royal New Zealand Returned and Services Association and some other submitters. New
Zealand First does not agree with the Government’s position. We strongly believe that
all military veterans who meet the el igibility criteria should be entitled to receive a
veterans’ pension in recognition that they have served their country. There should be a
clear distinction which acknowledges the important difference” —and this is a critical
point—“compared to receiving st andard New Zealand Superannuation. The additional
benefits of a veterans’ pension are relatively minor, but the sentiment and recognition is
vitally important to all those affected by this.” It is not just the money but the
recognition and the sentiment that go with it, to recognise that these people have served
their country.
It is also very disturbing that many veterans continue to struggle to receive their
various allowances and disability allowances, as a result of medical records tha t are
missing or are in error. And it is greatly disturbing that we had a situation this week
where the Rev. Wally Te Ua was in the High Court here in Wellington having to take
Veterans Affairs New Zealand and the Government to court to prove that he has c ancer
as a result of his deployment to Viet Nam and being affected by Agent Orange while in
the jungles of Viet Nam. It is incredible that a man like that, an Anglican vicar —an
Anglican vicar—has to take Veterans Affairs to court to try to prove that his c ancer was
a result of Agent Orange.
Back in 2008 I was at Tribute 08, the apology to the Viet Nam veterans here in
Wellington, which was held in this Chamber and in the Legislative Council Chamber.
The Rt Hon Helen Clark made the apology on behalf of the Government to the Viet
Nam veterans. At the Basin Reserve Lieutenant General Jerry Mateparae, the then Chief
of Defence Force, also apologised to them, and he also said that veterans will not be
17198 Veterans’ Support Bill 10 Apr 2014
disadvantaged because there were errors with medical records and because medical
records were missing. He said in his speech that the New Zealand Defence Force had let
them down. He said that it had let them down and they would not suffer as a result of
the medical records being missing or in error. That was Tribute  08, and yet 6 years later
many, many, many veterans —thousands of veterans —are still struggling to get what
they are due from Veterans Affairs New Zealand.
New Zealand First can assure the veterans —and some will be listening to this out
there today —that New Zealand First will rectify this. We will rectify this. We will
ensure that they get what they are due and that they are honoured in the right way by
this country. Those men and women who have put their bodies on the line, put their
lives on the line for this country, will be recognised in the true manner.
It is just very sad that so many National Party members of Parliament have not had
the same close experience with many of these veterans and with the military. I think it
comes from the top down. It would be nice to think that the Prime Minister and some of
those members could have some heart in this and say: “We will honour them, we will
do our best by them, and we will stop this once and for all.” New Zealand First will
support the Veterans’ Support Bill, but we will be speaking strongly in favour of sorting
out some of the aspects of it that need rectifying.

items.speaker: LOUISA WALL
items.text: Kia ora. Thank you very much for the
opportunity to contribute  to the second reading debate on the Veterans’ Support Bill,
which Labour supports. I want to acknowledge my colleagues who sit on the Social
Services Committee for the manner in which we normally conduct the discussions and
dialogue. It is fair to say tha t there have been intense discussion and dialogue
specifically about whether or not veterans should qualify for a veterans pension by
virtue of having a disability. I thought I would provide a little bit of history not only on
how we have come to where we are now but also on the whole philosophy about why
veterans have to have a disability to receive support.
What I wanted to do was pick up on my colleague Andrew Williams’ mention of
veterans who have specifically served our nation in Viet Nam, because it w as, in fact, a
2003 Health Committee inquiry into agent orange that started this process. One of the
findings of that particular Health Committee report was that we needed to review the
1954 War Pensions Act. What the Government then did at that stage was enter into a
memorandum of understanding with the Royal New Zealand Returned Services
Association and the Ex -Vietnam Services Association. Then in 2007 we instigated the
Law Commission review. So the momentum for the review of the 1954 Act and for the
piece of legislation that is here before us is now over 10 years old.
In terms of why you have to be disabled to receive any form of State assistance
actually goes back to a quote from Queen Elizabeth I: “ such as have adventured their
lives and lost their lim bs, or disabled their bodies in defence of Her Majesty and the
State, should be relieved and rewarded that they may reap the fruit of their good
deserving”. I repeat that —the fruit of their good deserving. What happened after that
speech was the formation of a charity called the Chatham Chest, which occurred in
1590. So the reality of the philosophy around why our veterans have to be disabled to
receive a veterans pension actually goes back to that undertaking —yes, which is
interesting—by Queen Elizabeth I.  So we have seen that philosophy just be transferred
historically.
What happened from that was that, in 1713, essentially, that is when the pension for
veterans was created. The same was replicated in the USA, which became a pension
plan for disabled vete rans, and that occurred in 1792. So, essentially, all New Zealand
has done to get to this point in time is to continue to perpetuate a charitable response to
veterans who have fought for our country and have become scarred by that experience
10 Apr 2014 Veterans’ Support Bill 17199
or disabled by that experience. I think the question we have to ask today is whether or
not that philosophy should drive the provision of a veterans pension now and into the
future.
I do want to look at the numbers. The Hon Phil Goff mentioned that currently we
have 16,700 veterans who would qualify. We have a lot of veterans within the 80 to
100-year age range. These are our veterans who served in World War II. But the
interesting statistic I want to share with the House from the regulatory impact statement,
which is d ated 27 September 2008, is that, in 5 years, 28 percent of those veterans
actually will not be alive any more. So that means of those 16,700, in 2019 we are
actually talking about only 12,000 veterans. So it is incumbent on the House, I think, to
challenge itself to be critical about the provision of services and of support to our
veterans, to understand the history of that provision, and, as I said before, to question
whether or not that is acceptable and relevant as we move into the future. Because
certainly both the Law Commission and the Royal New Zealand Returned and Services’
Association were very clear in their submissions that they could not see any rationale as
to why all qualifying veterans —and these are veterans who have gone over and risked
their lives and their limbs to serve our country and to protect all of us —should not
qualify for a veterans pension.
I actually think there is a compelling argument for this House to work together,
which is what we have tried to do in the select committee. To be forced as an
Opposition—and I know I stand here as a member of the Labour Party with our New
Zealand First colleagues and with our Green colleagues, as servants on the Social
Services Committee, trying very hard to get a consensus around this point. So we are
not playing politics, actually. What we are playing is a very straight bat, founded on a
Law Commission process —recommendation 95 —and founded on a fantastic
submission by the Royal New Zealand Returned and Services’ Association.
My colleague the Ho n Phil Goff as our veterans affairs spokesperson will be
proposing within the Committee stage a Supplementary Order Paper so that we can get
consensus and all of us, as a Parliament, can recognise that our veterans are worthy of
recognition. For a lot of t hem—and I am speaking on behalf of veterans from my
Manurewa RSA, and I have spoken to Graham Dolan, who is the president —they are
proud to have represented our country. It is a sense of pride for them to have a veterans
pension. Yes, there are going to be  benefits and additional support that they will get.
But I think they are not a charity any more. Our veterans do not need to be treated as a
charity any more. I guess my plea to the House and to the Opposition is to please have a
look at it. If we are to debate the Committee stage next week, we still have time to reach
consensus.
As I said before, if we actually put veterans at the centre of this bill —because, in
fact, the Veterans’ Affairs Act is all about meeting the needs of veterans. Mike Sabin
might think that is strange, but actually saying that someone has to have a disability to
get support and then haggling over the level of that support seems really disingenuous
when we say that we honour what they do. All of us on Anzac Day will be at the
services in our electorates, honouring the people who have risked their lives for us. I
think it is really disingenuous of us not to be really critical about why we will not open
our minds to a change in philosophy that is actually about recognising the contribu tion
that our veterans have made to our society, the contribution that our veterans continue to
make to our society, the sense of pride that we have in their achievements, and the sense
of contribution that we have within a global context for participating  in these wars to
bring peace to the world. So as a member of the select committee, it has been my
pleasure and my privilege to be involved in the passage of the bill through the House. I
look forward to further discussions and I commend the bill to the House. Thank you.
17200 Veterans’ Support Bill 10 Apr 2014

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: I am very pleased to take a call on this bill,
the Veterans’ Support Bill. There has been consensus across the Social Services
Committee on much of it. On  some of it we have parted our ways and views. One of
them is what the previous speaker, Louisa Wall, has just alluded to. As an ex - naval
officer myself, I can assure this House that no serviceman goes away to fight for their
country thinking “I wonder w hat I’ll get in the way of a veterans pension when I come
back.” or anything of that order.
What this bill is about in terms of the veterans pension is bringing parity from what
there was in 1954, because let us not forget that a lot of those people have since passed
on. To all of a sudden say that now there is only a few of them left, actually that
disability—and successive Governments have made decisions on this —that would have
given them the prerequisite opportunity to have that veterans pension should somehow
now mean nothing is wrong. It is wrong because of those who have been there before. I
can assure the House that there is not a single serviceman who serves their country
because of what they may get out of it —some minor financial compensation —at some
other stage in their life.
Having said that, of course it is important that every veteran is supported
wholeheartedly in a holistic way. Actually, that is why this House is largely in
agreement on everything else on this. What this bill does is ensure that no one is worse
off, that everyone is supported in a more tangible and realistic and modern way. But
never forget that servicemen do not do what they do for this.
Can I just also acknowledge the contribution of Major Rebecca Thornley. She got
promoted during this exercise, and I am sure she is going to shout at some stage shortly.
I also acknowledge Ross Miller for his contribution, and my father, Lew Sabin, and my
uncle Lew Gibb, who are also former servicemen. I am very proud to support this bill.
Bill read a second time.

sections.heading: Credit Contracts And Financial Services Law Reform Bill

items.text: Second Reading

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: I move, That the Credit
Contracts and Financial Services Law Reform Bill be now read a second time . I would
like to compliment the Commerce Committee for its consideration of this technically
challenging piece of legislation. The committee has considered approximately 70
submissions, covering a wide range of views, and tested the underlying policy intent of
the bill. The policy intent remains sound. The Commerce Committee’s report reflects
the large amount of work that has gone into getting the bill to this point. The b ill
comprehensively amends the consumer credit legislation, which is an important part of
the Business Growth Agenda, promoting confidence in our financial markets. The bill
reflects a sensible approach to compliance costs through amendments recommended by
the Commerce Committee, including changes to the standing disclosure requirements
and repossession provisions. It is not the intent of this legislation to reduce access to
credit by imposing heavy compliance costs that will ultimately be passed on to
consumers.
Many changes have been made to improve our consumer protections under this bill.
At the select committee, many submitters raised concerns about the protections
available, particularly to vulnerable consumers. The bill as introduced already elevated
consumer protection to the primary purpose of the Act and introduced the new concept
of responsible lending. It introduced sensible reforms, including that initial disclosure
must be provided before the contract is entered into. Standing disclosure must b e
available on request and free of charge. Overpayments must be refunded to the
10 Apr 2014 Credit Contracts and Financial Services Law Reform Bill 17201
borrower. Hardship applications can be made by borrowers who are already in default.
The Commerce Committee has helpfully refined many of these changes, and it is
pleasing to s ee the proposals in the bill confirmed and strengthened. The amendments
made by this bill ensure that the interests of consumers are protected, lenders compete
effectively, and consumers can participate confidently in the market.
The current law, the Cred it Contracts and Consumer Finance Act, is a principle -
based approach to consumer credit legislation. The lender responsibility principles will
help consumers and lenders to identify the practices you would expect from a
responsible lender. The responsible lending code is intended to provide guidance and
elaboration on the principles. Submissions to the committee asked that the status of the
code should be clearer. Submitters were also impatient for the code to come into force
as soon as possible. I share that impatience. We are keen to progress this legislation and
the code. As a result the committee has recommended that the bill specifies the code is
non-binding but also allows for work to begin on the code before the Act comes into
force. This will ensure that the principles and the code come into force at the same time:
no later than 12 months after the Act has passed, or, hopefully, sooner.
The fees provisions, particularly the provisions relating to unreasonable credit and
default fees, have been a cont roversial area of the bill. Submissions to the Commerce
Committee stated that the provisions needed work. The committee has recommended
that the bill make it clear that fees are constrained by a reasonableness test, and that the
test is anchored in the principle that fees are a means for creditors to recover costs. This
is consistent with the policy intention of the legislation as it currently stands. The
committee has recommended two further amendments to the fees provisions: firstly,
making it clear that prepayment fees should be limited to losses from changes in interest
rates for fixed rate contracts and, secondly, that third -party fees will also be subject to
the unreasonable fees test. They are in addition to the increased limitation period for
unreasonable fees that was included in the bill as introduced.
A significant improvement to the consumer credit landscape is the incorporation of
the Credit (Repossession) Act provisions into this bill. The 2012 Law Commission
report on credit repossession recom mended measures to provide a balance between
consumer protection and access to credit. The primary recommendation was to
incorporate repossession law into the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act.
Repossession is part of the life cycle of a loan, and the idea is that the law should deal
with the consumer credit as a whole. The bill adopts virtually all of the Law
Commission recommendations, and makes it clearer and easier for lenders and
borrowers alike to know where they stand in a repossession proces s. Goods available to
be repossessed must be specifically identified by the lender, and some items, including
beds, bedding, medical equipment, and heaters, will be prohibited from the repossession
altogether. Borrowers who have received a repossession war ning notice will also have
the right to voluntarily return the specified goods, rather than being forced to participate
in an often stressful repossession process. Previously the Credit (Repossession) Act was
self-regulated.
One of the most significant am endments in relation to credit repossession is the
introduction of the Commerce Commission as the regulator. Enforcement was a key
area identified in submissions to the committee where consumers and their advocates
called for action. The committee has take n a positive step in boosting enforcement
powers and penalties for breach. The committee has recommended the alignment of
penalties with the Fair Trading Act, increasing these from $30,000 to $200,000 for an
individual and from $30,000 to $600,000 for a co mpany, increasing the amount of
statutory damages available from $3,000 to $6,000, and introducing an infringement
regime that will allow the Commerce Commission to issue infringement notices in
17202 Credit Contracts and Financial Services Law Reform Bill 10 Apr 2014
respect of minor misconduct or straightforward issue of fact. In addition, where a lender
breaches the lender responsibility principles more than once, the court will be able to
order certain persons not to act as creditors. This will provide a mechanism for
recidivist and irresponsible lenders to be banned from the market.
I know that the select committee gave full consideration to the issue around interest
rate caps. I note that in its report it states that although restricting interest rates may
offer consumers protection from one form of high -cost credit, it con sidered that it may
also have unintended consequences. Those include restricting access to credit for
consumers and also having the interest rate that is at the upper limit coming to be
viewed as a target or reasonable. The committee considered that the pr ovisions included
in the bill, especially as they relate to disclosure, unreasonable fees, and responsible
lending, would reduce the risk of lenders offering unaffordable credit. I do agree with
the committee on those findings.
Also of note in the bill is  the increased access for consumers to the oppression and
hardship remedies. Access to justice is paramount when it comes to consumer
protection. Submitters noted that many consumers do not know where to go when they
are in trouble. The bill will allow app lications for hardship relief to be made once the
debtor is already in default, and elaborates on the grounds for a court to reopen a credit
contract on the grounds of oppression. The committee has recommended that specific
references in the financial disp ute resolution schemes are included within the Act,
increasing their presence.
To conclude, I commend the committee for its consideration and examination of this
bill. I believe this bill will be welcomed by lenders, borrowers, consumer g roups,
budget advisers, regulators, and the like. We want the consumer credit market to work
as effectively as possible. Reshaping the consumer lending environment is an important
part of the Government’s Business Growth Agenda. These changes will boost
confidence in the role that consumer credit plays in our financial markets while
providing increased protection for New Zealand’s most vulnerable consumers. I
commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: CAROL BEAUMONT
items.text: I am rising to support the Credit Contracts and
Financial Services Law Reform Bill at its second reading. This is a substantial bill and it
covers across the consumer credit area. Certainly, as the Minister of Consumer Affairs
has said, there are ma ny very positive provisions in this bill. For many of us, and, I am
sure, for those listening, the impact on fringe lending or predatory lending as part of
consumer credit is the area we are particularly interested in. I just want to look at what
that problem is, because, actually, it is a weeping sore. Just in the last month or so, there
have been reports in the media from budget services all around New Zealand of
examples of 100 percent interest rates, of 50 percent interest rates, and of 50 percent
interest rates for a loan of 7 days. These are just a few examples that I have recently
looked at. This is a real problem. People know —I am sure that virtually every MP in
this House knows —about the shonky business model of the so -called truck shops that
rattle around in low -income parts of our communities. So we know that there is a
problem and it is an ongoing one.
But it has got worse. In tough economic times the problem has got a lot worse. These
lenders—these predatory lenders —have preyed on vulnerable con sumers. They have
preyed on families who are struggling to make ends meet. There has been an increasing
problem of the type of predatory lender that has been in the market. So over recent years
we have seen an explosion in, for example, the number of pay -day lenders—short-term,
smaller loans, supposedly from one pay period to another but often longer than that —
loans by texting, and things like that. So there has been an increasing problem from new
players. Budget services say that the level of indebtedness that they see in our
10 Apr 2014 Credit Contracts and Financial Services Law Reform Bill 17203
communities has increased. The overwhelming majority of people who go into budget
services are tied up in high -interest consumer debt, and many of the budget services
have seen a change in the ratio —that is, the proportion of people wh om they see who
are in the paid workforce has increased, as well.
Families are damaged by these lenders. Families are damaged as they try to repay
excessive interest rates, and many of them actually repay those loans with those
excessive interest rates. Th at is just taking money that they can ill afford to lose out of
their children’s pockets or mouths —taking it away from feeding and clothing their
children. So it is being irresponsible not to have acted sooner when we know this
problem, when we can see the se problems, and I know that the level of concern in the
community is very, very high.
This particular bill has been a long time coming. There was already a review of
consumer credit laws under way when National came into Government. It started in
2007 with the Financial Summit held in South Auckland, and that was held in response
to concerns about the adequacy of the current legislation, the Credit Contracts and
Consumer Finance Act —particularly in response to its adequacy in dealing with
predatory loan s harks, which were starting to be seen as an increasing problem. The
deprioritisation of the work of reviewing that legislation is shameful. The delays,
despite the rhetoric from across the House of getting tough on loan sharks, has just been
truly shameful. I ask how many thousands of families have been caused immeasurable
grief and hardship as a consequence of the exploitation and predatory behaviour that has
been increasingly evident right across New Zealand, but it is especially evident in low -
income are as. Loan sharks, truck shops, and pay -day lenders have flourished in an
environment of low and static wages, ever -rising prices, and high unemployment. This
is not the rock star economy that the Prime Minister brags about.
I want to talk about interest ra te caps. The Minister has referred to them in his
speech. How many members of this House think that interest rates of 80 percent, 100
percent, 200 percent, or 700 percent are acceptable? How many of you think that that is
acceptable? How many of the people  listening to this debate think that those sorts of
rates are a fair go? If we went and surveyed New Zealanders, how many of those people
do you think would think that it is OK? Well, I do not think too many would. So why
are such rates legal and why are we not addressing those rates in this bill?
Although Labour welcomes many parts of the Credit Contracts and Financial
Services Law Reform Bill as it is a positive step to further protect consumers, we are
outraged that National has, once again, rejected in terest rate caps. New Zealand is now
one of the last remaining countries that have not capped rates in an effort to curb
unscrupulous rates of interest. Many of those paying such interest rates can ill afford to
lose that money from their impossibly tight family budgets. As I said, many of those
people repay those rates, but at what cost? It is at the cost of food, at the cost of
clothing, and at the cost of other essentials for their family, and many get caught in a
cycle of debt and despair that has a hug e cost for that whole family. Many are
vulnerable families living in our poorest communities.
On 1 July last year Australian legislation came into force capping interest rates at 48
percent right across Australia. A bill was introduced into the US Senate in April 2013
proposing an interest rate cap of 36 percent right across the United States. More than 80
percent of the individual states in the United States already had interest rate restrictions.
Britain was one of the last European jurisdictions to deci de to implement loan shark
interest rate caps. It had explored every avenue in an attempt to avoid caps, but just
before Christmas, Prime Minister Cameron and the Chancellor of the Exchequer,
George Osborne, did a U -turn and announced interest rate caps af ter previously
denouncing them. They announced that every avenue had been explored and that there
17204 Credit Contracts and Financial Services Law Reform Bill 10 Apr 2014
was simply no alternative to interest rate restrictions. In addition to the above, interest
rate restrictions now apply in Japan, Singapore, most countries in  Africa and Europe,
Canada, Mexico, and almost all of South America. This list is by no means exhaustive.
The same old tired arguments —and the Minister of Consumer Affairs had them just
before—were trotted out during consideration of this bill: unintended  consequences, the
caps become a target, access to credit from loan sharks may be reduced or driven
underground. What was not adequately answered for Labour was why this would be a
problem here in New Zealand but not in the many, many jurisdictions around the world
that have introduced interest rate caps. If the Government’s concerns have any
substance, then New Zealand would not stand out as one of the last remaining countries
not to have imposed interest rate caps. I personally challenge Minister Craig Fo ss to
find a country that has recently repealed such provisions because they have proved
unworkable. Canada has had them for 8 years. If they had all those consequences, why
has it not repealed that legislation?
So we are not going to sit back and leave t his unchallenged. We will be putting
forward amendments to this bill to include interest rate caps and also to ensure that the
oppression provisions can be used to look at interest rates. I am pleased to say that when
we introduced those, we had clear indications of support from the Greens, New Zealand
First, Mana, Brendan Horan, and the Māori Party. Peter Dunne is the man we need to
get across the line, I say to everybody. To those listening, Peter Dunne is the man we
need to get across the line. He supported interest rate caps when he voted for my
member’s bill in 2010. What stops him doing it now? He said at the time he was deeply
disappointed. What stops him, in my opinion, is his need for the National Party’s
support, and it outweighs anything else for that man, so I urge everybody to talk to Peter
Dunne. Let him know what you think he should do.
Going back to the rest of the bill, the bill contains many positive provisions, as I have
already said. Many of them have been provisions that budget services put forward years
ago and from citizens advice bureaux in the review Labour commenced 7 years ago. I
want to acknowledge the work of those people. They deal with the consequences of this
every single day.
My member’s bill also provided for responsible lending provisions in 2010,  and I am
pleased to see that we have responsible lending provisions, albeit 4 years later, in this
legislation. Another thing I am very pleased to see is responsible lending provisions
being applied to guarantors. I think that is great. I think that is pa rticularly good for all
those elderly people who end up guaranteeing loans for their children and their
grandchildren. Truck shops, as I have mentioned, will be covered by some of the
provisions, and I want to acknowledge my colleague Kris Faafoi. Kris and  I also
worked very hard on the select committee to try to ensure that truck shops were covered
by those provisions. Thank you.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: I am very pleased to stand and
speak in the second reading of the Credit Contracts and Financial Services Law Reform
Bill. I want to say thank you very much to the officials who worked alongside the
Commerce Committee. This was a particularly interesting but also a very complex a nd
large bill. In fact, the commentary that the committee signed off, as a record of our
work, was about 25 pages long —one of the largest commentaries, I think, in a bill this
year. It showed the complexity and the scope of the work that we did.
The availability of credit, both for businesses and for consumers, is fundamental to
the sound operation of a modern economy. Many goods and services are purchased
through consumer transactions that are partly or completely financed by credit. Without
credit, such purchases would not occur and consumers and businesses would be worse
10 Apr 2014 Credit Contracts and Financial Services Law Reform Bill 17205
off. Accessible consumer credit can make a significant contribution to the welfare of
consumers and to the prosperity of business.
The credit industry can be categorised in a number of ways. The Reserve Bank
household financial liabilities report from a year ago shows that there was
approximately, at that point in time, $180 billion of housing loans, $9 billion of bank
consumer loans, and $3.9 billion of non-bank consumer loans.
Colmar Brunton produced a report in 2011 for the Ministry of Consumer Affairs
entitled Using a third tier lender: experiences of New Zealand borrowers . This report
defined the three segments in the consumer credit market —that is, first -tier lenders,
second-tier l enders, and third -tier lenders. First -tier lenders include registered banks.
Second-tier lenders include building societies, credit unions, the Public Service
Investment Society, and other deposit-taking financial institutions. The third-tier lenders
are p roviders of personal non -mortgage credit, which are not banks, credit unions,
building societies, deposit-taking institutions, or credit card providers. Third-tier lenders
include finance companies, pay-day lenders, and moneylenders.
Some third-tier lenders are quite large organisations with multiple outlets. However,
most are single -outlet, small operations. Third -tier lenders have tended to focus their
business in lower -income areas. A number of lenders operate solely via the telephone,
internet, and/or brokers, and third -tier lenders are seeing opportunities and increasing
demands for more accessible loans that are not being met by the banks and other credit
providers. Third-tier lenders operate in a market where it is easier to engage in practices
that potentially take advantage of vulnerable consumers because many of the borrowers
have lower levels of financial literacy and/or have low incomes and do not have access
to affordable credit.
One of the things that we found quite challenging in the committe e was the marked
differentiation between those different tiers. That was quite a challenge, as we looked at
wanting to certainly address the real problem that happens, particularly in those low -
income families and communities where financial literacy is lo w. I think we worked
quite extensively in the committee to try to find those demarcations.
One of the areas that we worked on was lender responsibility principles. The bill
introduces the concept of responsible lending to New Zealand credit legislation,
requiring lenders to help borrowers to be reasonably aware. It does not take away the
responsibility of the borrower to gain financial literacy, but it puts the onus upon the
people lending the money to do everything they can to help the borrower to become
reasonably aware of the full implications of entering into a credit contract.
We recommend requiring lenders to express in plain language the terms of
agreements and subsequent variations to agreements, to help borrowers and guarantors
to reach informed decisions. This is a very important part of the bill. Its sounds simple,
but when we have a population—particularly in the northern part of the country—that is
increasingly made up of immigrants who have come from overseas and whose English
language may not  be as strong as it is in the rest of country, it is important that plain
language is used and that borrowers become reasonably aware of those implications.
There is much to cover on this, but I have probably said enough at this point in time.
I am very h appy to commend this excellent bill to the House and thank all the
Commerce Committee members for their hard work in getting it this far.

items.text: No, no, ethical behaviour and ethical standards are

10 Apr 2014 Credit Contracts and Financial Services Law Reform Bill 17207
Moving on, one thing I am particularly pleased about in this bill, for the benefit of
the Minister of Pacific Island Af fairs over there, if we look at the commentary under
“Content of continuing disclosure statement” —and we would love a bit of that when it
comes to the Minister of Justice, would we not, a bit of continuing disclosure —it is the
recommendation to insert new clause 13A, “to provide for regulations to prescribe a
minimum repayment warning on credit card statements.” This is something I am
particularly interested in —and I have campaigned in my own way over the years in
several committees about this —because, as t he commentary says, this is where “The
warning would detail to the debtor the consequences of paying only the minimum
monthly payment on credit card debt, such as higher interest costs over time.” The
Aussies have had this for several years.
When we talk about financial literacy, it is incumbent on this Parliament to assist
those who often cannot —sometimes will not, but often as not cannot —assist
themselves. I put it to the House that there is no better form of financial literacy than for
a bank to do as t hey do with mortgages, where they tell you on your statement what
your repayments are, what your interest bill is from month to month, what your interest
bill currently will be on maturity, and the total amount of the debt on maturity. You can
see it all mapped out and see how many years you have to pay it off.
Yet banks in New Zealand, for a time, have resisted under really the only excuse,
which is cost. There is a cost to making these changes, and I acknowledge that, but it is
not an earth -shattering one. Their parent companies in Australia were compelled some
years ago to disclose to a person who holds a credit card that this is your minimum
payment, this is the average payment you are making monthly, and that if you keep
paying it off with this frequency it will take X number of years and you will have paid
X amount of money, you will have paid the bank a bucketload of interest, and it might
take you 10 years to pay it off. At that point everything is disclosed to the person who is
incurring that debt.
I would wager—I hope I am right—that many people, once that explicit disclosure is
made on the credit card statement, will look at it and go: “Heck. I didn’t think if I kept
paying at this sort of frequency that I would be paying t hat amount of interest and that it
would take that amount of time, and my total bill at the end of this would be a
bucketload of cash.” Once that realisation is made, I suspect those people will say:
“Hey, I’m going to remedy this. I’m not going to give th e bank a bucketload of money
in interest. I’m actually going to shape up in terms of my internal financial processes.
I’m going to redo my household budget, and I’m going to try to quit this debt or
minimise it to a manageable level.”
I am quite proud of that. I am pleased, and I am grateful to all members of the
committee. It was something that I think sprang out from left field for us all. We raised
it with the officials. I commend our officials, who went away and challenged the banks
and the financial institutions and came back with a remedy. Yes, it will put a bit of cost
on the banks to make the electronic changes that they will have to make. It will not raise
interest rates. I would say that I would be very surprised if it is passed on in any major
shape or form to the punters, to the customers, but it will bring our banks in line with
their Australian parents. More than many things that have been done around financial
literacy, to me this is one of the ultimate forms of it because it is completely transparent,
it hides nothing, and it gives a warts and all view to the person who is incurring debt
through a credit card.
We certainly know that it is relatively easy for credit cards to be made available to
people and we know that they are an easy form fo r all of us who like to make the odd
purchase from time to time. They are an easy form that aids our purchasing power. For
those who can afford it, that is OK. For those who cannot afford it, it is troublesome. I
17208 Credit Contracts and Financial Services Law Reform Bill 10 Apr 2014
am one of those people who can afford to pa y the credit card off on time, every time.
The banks do not particularly like me, I suspect, because they do not get any interest out
of it. I am well remunerated, like all members of this House.
