items.speaker: JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: The Green Party is happy to vote in support of
the Credit Contracts and Financial Services Law Reform Bill at its second reading. The
Green Party has long called for be tter regulation of third -tier lenders—that is, pay -day
lenders, moneylenders, and those who are known as loan sharks. Third -tier lending at
extortionate interest rates has been increasing in New Zealand and in other jurisdictions
over the past decade. It i s both a symptom and a cause of growing inequality. The gap
between those who have and those who have not is growing in New Zealand and in
other countries, and wealth is being concentrated in the hands of fewer people.
Post the global financial crisis, al though the people who arguably caused the global
financial crisis—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am sorry to interrupt the
member. There is this banter going across the House. I am trying to hear th e member
who is speaking.

items.speaker: JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker. Post the global
financial crisis, a number of people lost their jobs and they found it more difficult to put
food on the table and to pay their ever -increasing power bills. Predatory lenders set up
precisely in those areas of greatest social and economic deprivation and take advantage
of limited financial literacy and a desperate need for cash to make ends meet.
It is not enough to improve financial literacy a nd regulate loan sharks alone. Part of
the solution is addressing the underlying causes of this growing inequality, and that
means taking a hard look at our tax system, which currently favours the wealthy few.
We need to look after our children, 250,000 of  whom are living in poverty. There are
many steps the Government can take to do this thing, like raising the minimum wage,
paying a living wage themselves and working towards a living wage across the country,
and investing in smart, affordable transport an d kid-friendly streets. Our Schools at the
Heart policy, which is focused on our education hubs and on making sure that kids are
looked after from the beginning, is going to help deal with some of this growing
inequality.
But the immediate issue of regula ting third-tier lenders is finally being addressed in
this bill. Even though we do not agree with everything in the bill —there are a few areas
where we certainly differed from the Government’s policy, and that is expressed in the
minority report—we are very happy to finally see the very good work that was done as
an outcome of the review of the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act. I have to
acknowledge the excellent work of officials in this area, and especially the work of my
colleague Carol Beaumont on the Commerce Committee. She is really the expert in this
area. I am certainly not. I had to look to her expertise. She advocated for really
important changes in this bill, and I was so happy that she was there to do that.
We will see truck shops and o ther lenders covered by this legislation, which is
incredibly important. As Carol Beaumont said in her speech earlier this evening, one of
the biggest disappointments of this legislation is that it does not include any provision
for setting a cap on intere st rates. What is disappointing is that we did not get any
10 Apr 2014 Credit Contracts and Financial Services Law Reform Bill 17209
compelling evidence or reasons why this was not being included in the bill. We
certainly asked for it. We heard a huge number of submissions, and it is fair to say that
some submitters were not in favour of interest rate caps —most notably the Bankers’
Association. But there were quite a few submitters who were in favour, and there
certainly is a lot of evidence that other jurisdictions are using interest rate caps to
protect consumers from spirallin g, out-of-control debt. As Carol Beaumont said, New
Zealand is one of the last remaining countries not to have a provision for interest rate
caps.
So although I am certain that the provisions in this bill will go some way to
protecting those consumers who  are most vulnerable, I am concerned that we have not
given ourselves even the opportunity to try interest rate caps. The reasons given for not
including interest rate caps were simply that there might potentially be a lack of access
to short -term credit a nd that the interest rate cap would become the target and
everybody would automatically put up interest rates to whatever the cap was. I have to
say, these are not really overwhelmingly compelling reasons for not including some sort
of provision. I am an e mpiricist. I very much believe that we cannot know everything
before trying it—
Simon O’Connor: Did you say an imperialist?

items.speaker: JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: Empiricist.
Simon O’Connor: Oh, I thought you said imperialist.

items.speaker: JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: No, empiricist, sorry. So, basically, I think that when it
comes to policy, it is very easy to make up reasons for not trying something, but,
actually, if most of our trading partners in other comparable jurisdic tions are doing
something, then maybe we should give ourselves the opportunity to at least try it.
Seeing as how it took so many years for this legislation to come before the House, we
are not going to easily have that ability to include a cap in the futur e. I mean, it takes
time. We consulted on it. It was certainly spoken about in the submissions process. This
was the logical place to at least introduce the possibility of the Government imposing an
interest rate cap or allowing the Reserve Bank to set one.
Of course, if all these hypothetical drawbacks of interest caps did occur and there
were no other means of introducing them, then we could always roll it back, but we
should at least try it because it is an important tool. Why would you restrict the num ber
of tools in your tool kit to deal with predatory lenders? As we know, it is a growing
problem and one that is increasingly affecting the people in New Zealand who are the
most vulnerable and the people whom we should be looking out for the most.
The l ack of access to short -term credit is perhaps something that the Government
should be seeking to address so that those who have the least really should not be forced
to go out and get a pay -day loan, or a short -term loan, in order to put food on the table.
That should not be a reason. You should not need access to credit to get your kids
enough food to eat or to make sure that they have got warm clothes or that you are able
to pay your power bill. There are other problems, deeper problems, that need to be
addressed in this country, and I think that allowing predatory lenders to go out and
charge interest rates of well over 100 percent to people who have potentially —and I
have to say that most people are not very good at understanding compounding interest.
People who are struggling just to get enough to eat and to put food on the table might
not be in the best position to understand the consequences of interest rates that are
expressed simply in a daily rate and to understand what that is going to mean as it
compounds.
So, simply put, I think the Green Party is happy to see this legislation finally come to
its second reading. It is mostly very, very good, and we are disappointed that the
17210 Credit Contracts and Financial Services Law Reform Bill 10 Apr 2014
Government, for quite ideological reasons, seems to have neglected to inc lude an
important tool in the tool kit to address the problems we face.
The other disappointing thing, I think, was the last-minute amendments around credit
and default fees that were made entirely at the behest of the New Zealand Bankers’
Association—with some scaremongering claims that I am sure it made about the
increased costs to it. Again, I thought it was disappointing that the amendments came at
the last minute. We were not presented with very compelling evidence for the wording
changes. I think that although we have to admit that at least the Government did see this
legislation come before the House —that is good —and there are some improvements,
ultimately there are still some ideological policy decisions being made by the National
Government that ar e about “Let’s look after the bankers and let’s ideologically be
opposed to caps on interest rates, even though they might help those who are the most
vulnerable in our society.” Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon Peseta SAM LOTU -IIGA
items.text: It is a
pleasure to speak on this, the second reading of the Credit Contracts and Financial
Services Law Reform Bill. This bill will make a difference, and it wil l make a real
difference to people up and down this country who have fallen prey to predatory
moneylenders. Many of my colleagues and members opposite have referred to this. Part
of this bill is about protecting the most vulnerable in our communities in wh at is
sometimes the most desperate of times. The bill is a result of many hours of
consultation. I want to thank the officials as well. I also want to thank the Ministers,
both the present Minister of Consumer Affairs, Craig Foss, and past Ministers of
Consumer Affairs—Simon Bridges, who is in the House, and Simon Power —and many
others who have brought this bill to this stage. I also just want to say that the bill has
taken some of the clauses from my own member’s bill, which I launched 3 years ago —I
am qui te happy to tell my friends opposite —especially around credit repossession
agents. It is a bill that is going to make a difference to our lives and the lives of many
New Zealanders.
We campaigned on this bill in 2011. It is now seeing some real results and  I am glad
that members opposite have chosen to support it. What they have not spoken about is
the responsible lending guidelines that will be part of this bill.

items.speaker: Carol Beaumont
items.text: I did actually mention that.

items.speaker: Hon Peseta SAM LOTU -IIGA
items.text: No, they have talked a lot about interest rate caps
and I will come to that soon. The guidelines are about the duty on responsible lenders to
their borrowers and customers. They cannot be indifferent to the needs of those
borrowers. Th ey cannot be indifferent to the circumstances of those borrowers. They
cannot be indifferent to the borrowers who have situations where the transaction may
lead to distress. This bill will fundamentally change the way that lending is done in this
country a nd it will skew the power, if you like, back to protecting consumers,
particularly those vulnerable borrowers whom I referred to. I have seen them in my
electorate office and I have had family members who, sadly, have been fleeced by these
loan sharks. This bill is only part of the overall thrust of our Government to assist those
borrowers. It is about education, it is about having freephone lines so that they can
access help, and it is about the Commerce Commission playing its role in enforcing and
prosecuting these lenders. That is what it will be about in the future. Responsible
lending guidelines are going to be a critical part of this bill.
I just want to touch on interest rate caps, which members opposite have been
referring to. As I asked in a member’s bill that advocated for interest rate caps —and
they still do not get it across the aisle —what happens when you cap interest rates and
fees get out of control? What happens when default fees get out of control? What they
should be advocating—and I do not hear it—is a cost of finance cap, not an interest rate
10 Apr 2014 Credit Contracts and Financial Services Law Reform Bill 17211
cap. If you understand the fundamental difference between fees and interest rates, then
you would not be advocating the latter. What I am saying to members opposite is that
interest rate caps do not work. In the jurisdictions that have implemented them, you still
have predatory lending. It is a blunt instrument that does not work.
This bill has a lot of solutions. We are glad members opposite are supporting the
measures with in this bill because it is going to make a real difference to New
Zealanders out there that finally a Government —not the Labour Government but the
National Government—is putting in place these measures.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: I take a call on behalf of New Zealand First on
the Credit Contracts and Financial Services Law Reform Bill. It is very appropriate to
come after the Minister of Pacific Island Affairs, Sam Lotu -Iiga, with whom I had a
discussion today on this very subject. I asked the Minister whether he would reconsider
the aspect of capping the interest rates. He advised me that that was not going to be
possible, and he gave me various reasons. I am somewhat disappointed, Minister,
because you come from the very area that is one of the most affected by loan sharks, by
high interest rates, and by racketeers. The people whom you represent and are Minister
of desperately need all the protection that they can get. They are the most vulnerable,
the Pasifika people. My colleague here, Le’aufa’amulia Asenati Lole -Taylor, can
confirm that in the area of South Auckland, in the Manukau area, these people are very
vulnerable. They need every assistance to ensure that they are not ripped off by some of
these racketeers.
So it is disappointing that the National Government just cannot see fit to go that extra
step. It is bringing this bill through, but it cannot go that extra step to put caps on
interest rates. Caps have been introduced in the UK, the USA, Ca nada, Japan, Australia,
and much of Europe. This Government says it sees no justification for doing it here in
New Zealand, yet so many of our major trading partners, so many of the countries that
we have some of the closest contact with, have done this. T herefore, there can be no
justification for this Government saying it does not think it is appropriate to do it when
so many of these other countries, based on a huge amount of case studies and past
history in this area, have seen fit to do so.
It is also  most concerning that this bill will go through but that the suggested
amendments from Carol Beaumont in relation to those caps will be lost 61 votes to 60.
They will be lost by one vote. They will be lost by the one vote of the Hon Peter Dunne.
I use the word “honourable” very loosely, because in this case if he was to do the
honourable thing, he would vote for the amendments, as he voted back in 2010 for  the
Credit Reforms (Responsible Lending) Bill, a member’s bill that was then in the name
of Carol Beau mont. Back then United Future voted in favour of that bill, and that bill
said: “The amendments to the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act 2003 will
require lenders to seriously consider the actual means of a prospective borrower and
their ability to  service the debt and will allow for the prescription of maximum annual
percentage rates of interest payable in respect of consumer credit contracts. Rules
applying caps to annual interest rates now apply in many overseas countries, including
the United States, Canada and Australia.” That was in that bill, and the vote on that bill
was lost by 59 votes to 63, but those who voted for it included United Future.
So the Hon Peter Dunne was happy to vote for that and have caps 3 years ago, but
yet recently in t he media he has said that he has never supported it and never did
support it. He has done the usual flip -flop of a Minister. As the Rt Hon Winston Peters
said in the case of Peter Dunne, “he will double -cross that bridge when he comes to it.”
In this case he has double -crossed the bridge when he has come to it, because he is on
record—and I have a letter here also confirming it —saying that he supported that bill
and was sorry that it did not go through. He wrote a letter, and I have got the letter here.
17212 Credit Contracts and Financial Services Law Reform Bill 10 Apr 2014

items.speaker: He said
items.text: “I was very pleased to hear from you … thank you for taking the time to write
to me and for your [kindness]. I was happy to support this bill and was very sorry that it
did not proceed past first reading. I hope that further progress will be made on this issue
in future.” Well, this is the future, Peter Dunne —this is the future. This is 2014. We
now have a bill that would allow, if the Government accepted the amendments, caps to
go on interest rates.
At a time when people can be absolutely ripped off  with interest rates rising to three
digits—hundreds of percent —why should poor, vulnerable people be paying interest
rates of hundreds of percent, in some cases, when this Government has the ability to
support putting caps on interest rates? It is just ab solutely diabolical in this day and age
that this Government cannot see sense in doing this when our trans -Tasman sister
country, Australia, has done it, and when so many of these financial people operate on
both sides of the Tasman as well. Why should the y have constraints in Australia but not
have constraints here in New Zealand? It does not make sense. Why does this
Government often say “Oh, we are trying to harmonise with Australia as much as we
can so that businesses both sides of the Tasman know what the rules are and so do the
banks and everybody else —you know, so we’re harmonised.”, and yet here is an
instance where the Government will not harmonise with what is happening in Australia?
It is just absolutely nonsensical.
In the case of the Hon Peter Dunne, New Zealand First can say to him that once
again he is selling out, taking the baubles of office, and giving the one vote that is
required to stop those caps going in. If he followed what his party’s principles stand
for—and also we have confirmatio n that people within United Future are saying that
they would like to see these caps in place. They cannot understand why Peter Dunne
himself is not supporting the capping of rates. Peter Dunne is obviously a one -man
show, voting for his own self -interest, and not voting on the basis of what many of the
people in his own party would say. He is basically voting to ensure that he keeps his
ministerial portfolios, his Crown limousine, and all the baubles of office, so he will give
the one necessary vote to ensure that credit caps are not put on interest rates.
In closing, New Zealand First will just say once again that we are very disappointed.
We will be supporting the bill overall because it does significantly help vulnerable
people. It will enhance the whol e situation in terms of those who are most affected and
who require credit. But at the same time, when the bill comes through the Committee
stage we will be expressing grave concerns as to why the Government is, once again,
letting down low and middle inco me earners in this country and is not seeing sense by
doing that.

items.speaker: KANWALJIT SINGH BAKSHI
items.text: It is my pleasure to take a call on the
Credit Contracts and Financial Services Law Refo rm Bill. I would like to acknowledge
the Hon Simon Bridges and the Hon Craig Foss for their contributions to this bill. I
would also like to thank all the members of the Commerce Committee —in particular,
the Hon Peseta Sam Lotu -Iiga and Alfred Ngaro —for th eir contributions during the
select committee process. It is a very important bill, particularly for the people of South
Auckland, where I have got my office. It is my pleasure to commend this bill to the
House.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: Thank you very much for the chance to speak in
this second reading of the Credit Contracts and Financial Services Law Reform Bill.
Like the Minister of Pacific Island Affairs, Sam Lotu -Iiga, I also represent a community
that is disproportionately affected by the kind of behaviour that is carried on by third -
tier lenders—or, as we like to colloquially call them, loan sharks —and the likes of, as I
guess they would call themselves, mobile traders, whom we like to call truck shops.
10 Apr 2014 Credit Contracts and Financial Services Law Reform Bill 17213
It would not seem fair to any fair -minded New Zealander that interest rates of the
likes of 50 percent to 100 percent, or even more, are charged to vulnerable people in our
community. I think if you asked any fair -minded New Zealander who wants a fair g o
for consumers, especially those who are vulnerable and who cannot get credit from the
likes of traditional banks, they would say that getting charged the likes of 50 to 100
percent is just not fair. It lands a whole lot of families —and, as I say, there a re a whole
lot of families in my community who sign up to those kinds of deals —in massive
trouble. It usually ends up with them going to the likes of the local citizens advice
bureau or the Porirua Budget Service. I am going to see the Agape Budgeting Serv ice
tomorrow in Porirua. Those are the kinds of people who end up dealing with the hurt of
the families because the likes of third -tier lenders, or loan sharks, are able to charge
exorbitant interest rates.
Although we are supporting this piece of legisla tion, this is a massive opportunity
gone for this Government to take some real action to introduce interest rate caps. I do
want to acknowledge my colleague Carol Beaumont, who has a number of
Supplementary Order Papers on this bill. One of those specifica lly does do what the
Government should have done in the introduction of this bill, and that is to look at
interest rate caps. I think it was Mr Lotu -Iiga who said that these interest rate caps do
not work. So maybe Mr Lotu -Iiga would like to ask the likes of many countries in
Europe, Mexico, Canada, South Africa, Japan, Singapore —which has a Government
that this Government always says is doing a good job financially —the US, Australia,
and, most recently, the United Kingdom as to why they think it is appropr iate to put in
interest rate caps for third -tier lenders. I think those Governments probably recognise
the fact that there is huge public interest in making sure that the most vulnerable in our
communities are not stung more by the likes of interest rates of 50 percent to 100
percent.
Essentially, what we are saying here is that this side of the House is not OK with the
most vulnerable people in our community going to third -tier lenders and paying interest
rates of 50 percent to 100 percent or more. But th at side of the House —the
Government; National, United Future —are quite OK with people who probably cannot
afford to take out these loans having these huge, exorbitant interest rates. That is exactly
what this boils down to. We are not OK with it, but that Government is OK with it.
From now on, all the hurt that the likes of budgeting services see around the country
can be blamed on that Government because it is quite OK with letting things go on as
they are now.
Or, one person in this House, the Hon Peter Dunne, could change his mind again. He
could change his mind again. Andrew Little said that Mr Dunne supported a member’s
bill back in 2010 in the name of Carol Beaumont that would have introduced interest
rate caps. I want to quote from the same letter that Mr Little—

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: Williams.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: —Mr Williams, thank you —quoted from. I want to declare
somewhat of a conflict of interest. This letter is to Mr Andrew Shann, who is a
constituent of mine and who also works for me part -time, and who has been
campaigning against third-tier lenders since well into the past, and also to make sure
that interest rate caps come in.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: Ah!

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: You can crow over there, because you guys are OK with 50 percent
or 100 percent interest rates. You are OK with it. I am not OK with it. You guys are the
ones who are OK with it. I just want to say that Mr Dunne was not OK with it 4 years
ago. He said: “I was very pleased to hear from you … thank you for taking the time to
17214 Credit Contracts and Financial Services Law Reform Bill 10 Apr 2014
write to me” He said he supported the bill and was very sorry that it did not pass the
first reading.
So 4 years ago Mr Dunne was not OK with exorbitant interest rates, but now that he
has got the Crown car back and he is back in his ministerial office, he is toeing the party
line and he is all of a sudden not OK with caps on interest rates. I would suggest —if
people are watching this debate, and I am sure a lot of people around the country who
are interested in making sure that—

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: If they know you’re speaking, they will be—they will be.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: He is a retiring member. Those people who are interested in
making sure we are looking after vulnerable people can  put a lot of pressure on Mr
Dunne to change his mind again. His is the one vote that could change this whole thing.
Peter Dunne said in 2010 that he was OK with interest rate caps, but now that he is back
in the House with the Government, he is not OK with it.
So write letters to Peter.Dunne@parliament.govt.nz. Send him a letter —to the Hon
Peter Dunne. It is freepost. If you are not OK with 50 to 100 percent or more interest
rates, write Peter Dunne a letter, send him an email, or bombard his office with phone
calls. He is the one who can change this whole situation. The Government has not
shown any leadership on this. It is dead against interest rate caps. It does not want to
introduce them. But there is one person in this House who can change everything.  I fear
that he may not change his mind, because what did he do with asset sales? He made
sure he voted for that. That squeaked through with one vote. But I do not want to
discourage people from trying to get Peter Dunne to change his mind on this.
Can I just take a brief moment, because this was the first substantive piece of
legislation that I sat through on the Commerce Committee, to thank other members of
the Commerce Committee. It was a relatively good process. We had the odd stoush —
nothing compared with what we have had recently.

items.speaker: Carol Beaumont
items.text: Officials.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: Can I thank the officials too because, as the chair of the select
committee, Jonathan Young, said, the bill is very technical, but I think the way the
officials guided us through this process made it very plain sailing for someone who had
to make sense of this as a new member to the select committee.
I do represent a community where the effects of loan sharks and truck shops do have
a disproportionate effe ct. Although I support this piece of legislation, I do think, as I
have said before, that we have missed an opportunity to make the lives of those people
better. I have had people in my office who have been in tears because of the interest
rates and the debt that they have got themselves into with loan sharks. I cannot do much
more than offer the services of a budgetary advice service. That is heartbreaking
because I think this Parliament should be able to do something to prevent people from
getting into th ose situations. I think an interest rate cap certainly would have been one
of those ways.
There is also one person I do want to thank who is not in this House any more, and
that is Charles Chauvel. Before he left this House he also took a very strong lead ership
role in the Ōhariu electorate, which Mr Dunne is the MP for, in making sure that this
issue was brought to the fore. It was actually 5 years ago, when the effects of the global
financial crisis started kicking in, that this really started to hit home, especially with our
most vulnerable people in our communities.
As Sam Lotu-Iiga said, he put in a member’s bill 3 years ago —3 years ago. It was 3
years ago, and we are sitting here today, 6 months before an election, and something is
being done about it only now. My ques tion is why it has taken so long for this
Government to get off its chuff and make sure that something is done for these most
vulnerable people. We have still got the Committee stage of this debate to go, and I
10 Apr 2014 Credit Contracts and Financial Services Law Reform Bill 17215
suggest that that question may be a very stro ng theme in that debate —as to why it took
so long for this Government to do something. During that time a lot of families up and
down this country, and certainly in my electorate of Mana, have been put through harm
that I do not think they necessarily should have been put through. They are in debt. That
affects their daily lives. It affects what they can do with their kids and their families. If
this Government had acted a little bit sooner to put some protections in place for them,
their lives could have been markedly different.
I just want to finish up with this thing. There is one vote in this House that can
change it. We on this side of the House are not OK with interest rates of 50 to 100
percent or more. If this Government does not support the Supplementary Order Paper of
Carol Beaumont, that pretty much says that that Government is OK with it.
Bill read a second time.

items.text: In light of the State reception that is

THURSDAY, 10 APRIL 2014 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
BUSINESS STATEMENT 
Hon GERRY BROWNLEE (Leader of the House) : When the House resumes on 
Tuesday, 15 April the Government will look to progress a number of bills on the Order 
Paper, including the Vulnerable Children Bill, the Victims of Crime Reform Bill, and 
the Victims’ Orders Against Violent Offenders Bill. On Wednesday, 16 April, effective 
on the mo rning of Thursday 17 April and with the agreement of the Business 
Committee, the House will sit in extended hours to progress further Treaty of Waitangi 
settlement legislation. 
GRANT ROBERTSON (Labour—Wellington Central): I thank the Leader of the 
House for that update. I just wonder whether he could confirm that when we reach the 
next members’ day, the Government will ensure speedy progress to allow Sue 
Moroney’s Parental Leave and Emplo yment Protection (Six Months’ Paid Leave) 
Amendment Bill to have the airing in the House it deserves. 
Hon GERRY BROWNLEE (Leader of the House) : That is a rather confusing 
request to come from the shadow Leader of the House. I note that yesterday the 
Opposition, in fact, stalled the day by asking questions to members and, further, put in a 
letter to the Speaker seeking an additional hour -long special debate. Then, after years of 
saying this is the fastest-legislating Government in the West, it said we need to actually 
stop going quickly or go even more quickly. So what is the position of the Opposition?

One of the key changes made by the committee is to the threshold for the veterans 
pension. Submissions questioned whether 55 percent was the  appropriate level of 
whole-person impairment to use as a threshold for the veterans pension and other 
entitlements, noting that it did not appear to be the equivalent of the threshold currently 
used in the 1954 Act. The information that was provided to th e committee established 
that 52 percent whole -person impairment was, in fact, the most equivalent threshold,

bill has been amended to provide that a veteran or other claimant who currently meets

statements of principle as the main reference point for deciding claims. The statements

needed element of certainty to the process.

reported back by the committee. I commend this bill to the House.

Hon CRAIG FOSS (Minister of Consumer Affairs) : I move, That the Credit 
Contracts and Financial Services Law Reform Bill be now read a second time . I would 
like to compliment the Commerce Committee for its consideration of this technically 
challenging piece of legislation. The committee has considered approximately 70 
submissions, covering a wide range of views, and tested the underlying policy intent of 
the bill. The policy intent remains sound. The Commerce Committee’s report reflects 
the large amount of work that has gone into getting the bill to this point. The b ill 
comprehensively amends the consumer credit legislation, which is an important part of 
the Business Growth Agenda, promoting confidence in our financial markets. The bill 
reflects a sensible approach to compliance costs through amendments recommended by  
the Commerce Committee, including changes to the standing disclosure requirements 
and repossession provisions. It is not the intent of this legislation to reduce access to 
credit by imposing heavy compliance costs that will ultimately be passed on to 
consumers.  
Many changes have been made to improve our consumer protections under this bill. 
At the select committee, many submitters raised concerns about the protections 
available, particularly to vulnerable consumers. The bill as introduced already elevated  
consumer protection to the primary purpose of the Act and introduced the new concept 
of responsible lending. It introduced sensible reforms, including that initial disclosure 
must be provided before the contract is entered into. Standing disclosure must b e 
available on request and free of charge. Overpayments must be refunded to the 
10 Apr 2014 Credit Contracts and Financial Services Law Reform Bill 17201 
borrower. Hardship applications can be made by borrowers who are already in default. 
The Commerce Committee has helpfully refined many of these changes, and it is 
pleasing to s ee the proposals in the bill confirmed and strengthened. The amendments 
made by this bill ensure that the interests of consumers are protected, lenders compete 
effectively, and consumers can participate confidently in the market.  
The current law, the Cred it Contracts and Consumer Finance Act, is a principle -
based approach to consumer credit legislation. The lender responsibility principles will 
help consumers and lenders to identify the practices you would expect from a 
responsible lender. The responsible lending code is intended to provide guidance and 
elaboration on the principles. Submissions to the committee asked that the status of the 
code should be clearer. Submitters were also impatient for the code to come into force 
as soon as possible. I share that impatience. We are keen to progress this legislation and 
the code. As a result the committee has recommended that the bill specifies the code is 
non-binding but also allows for work to begin on the code before the Act comes into 
force. This will ensure that the principles and the code come into force at the same time: 
no later than 12 months after the Act has passed, or, hopefully, sooner.  
The fees provisions, particularly the provisions relating to unreasonable credit and 
default fees, have been a cont roversial area of the bill. Submissions to the Commerce 
Committee stated that the provisions needed work. The committee has recommended 
that the bill make it clear that fees are constrained by a reasonableness test, and that the 
test is anchored in the principle that fees are a means for creditors to recover costs. This 
is consistent with the policy intention of the legislation as it currently stands. The 
committee has recommended two further amendments to the fees provisions: firstly, 
making it clear that prepayment fees should be limited to losses from changes in interest 
rates for fixed rate contracts and, secondly, that third -party fees will also be subject to 
the unreasonable fees test. They are in addition to the increased limitation period for 
unreasonable fees that was included in the bill as introduced.  
A significant improvement to the consumer credit landscape is the incorporation of 
the Credit (Repossession) Act provisions into this bill. The 2012 Law Commission 
report on credit repossession recom mended measures to provide a balance between 
consumer protection and access to credit. The primary recommendation was to 
incorporate repossession law into the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act. 
Repossession is part of the life cycle of a loan, and the idea is that the law should deal 
with the consumer credit as a whole. The bill adopts virtually all of the Law 
Commission recommendations, and makes it clearer and easier for lenders and 
borrowers alike to know where they stand in a repossession proces s. Goods available to 
be repossessed must be specifically identified by the lender, and some items, including 
beds, bedding, medical equipment, and heaters, will be prohibited from the repossession 
altogether. Borrowers who have received a repossession war ning notice will also have 
the right to voluntarily return the specified goods, rather than being forced to participate 
in an often stressful repossession process. Previously the Credit (Repossession) Act was 
self-regulated.  
One of the most significant am endments in relation to credit repossession is the 
introduction of the Commerce Commission as the regulator. Enforcement was a key 
area identified in submissions to the committee where consumers and their advocates 
called for action. The committee has take n a positive step in boosting enforcement 
powers and penalties for breach. The committee has recommended the alignment of 
penalties with the Fair Trading Act, increasing these from $30,000 to $200,000 for an 
individual and from $30,000 to $600,000 for a co mpany, increasing the amount of 
statutory damages available from $3,000 to $6,000, and introducing an infringement 
regime that will allow the Commerce Commission to issue infringement notices in 
17202 Credit Contracts and Financial Services Law Reform Bill 10 Apr 2014 
respect of minor misconduct or straightforward issue of fact. In addition, where a lender 
breaches the lender responsibility principles more than once, the court will be able to 
order certain persons not to act as creditors. This will provide a mechanism for 
recidivist and irresponsible lenders to be banned from the market.  
I know that the select committee gave full consideration to the issue around interest 
rate caps. I note that in its report it states that although restricting interest rates may 
offer consumers protection from one form of high -cost credit, it con sidered that it may 
also have unintended consequences. Those include restricting access to credit for 
consumers and also having the interest rate that is at the upper limit coming to be 
viewed as a target or reasonable. The committee considered that the pr ovisions included 
in the bill, especially as they relate to disclosure, unreasonable fees, and responsible 
lending, would reduce the risk of lenders offering unaffordable credit. I do agree with 
the committee on those findings.  
Also of note in the bill is  the increased access for consumers to the oppression and 
hardship remedies. Access to justice is paramount when it comes to consumer 
protection. Submitters noted that many consumers do not know where to go when they 
are in trouble. The bill will allow app lications for hardship relief to be made once the 
debtor is already in default, and elaborates on the grounds for a court to reopen a credit 
contract on the grounds of oppression. The committee has recommended that specific 
references in the financial disp ute resolution schemes are included within the Act, 
increasing their presence. 
 To conclude, I commend the committee for its consideration and examination of this 
bill. I believe this bill will be welcomed by lenders, borrowers, consumer g roups, 
budget advisers, regulators, and the like. We want the consumer credit market to work 
as effectively as possible. Reshaping the consumer lending environment is an important 
part of the Government’s Business Growth Agenda. These changes will boost 
confidence in the role that consumer credit plays in our financial markets while 
providing increased protection for New Zealand’s most vulnerable consumers. I 
commend this bill to the House.

The availability of credit, both for businesses and for consumers, is fundamental to

credit, such purchases would not occur and consumers and businesses would be worse

the Hon Simon Bridges and the Hon Craig Foss for their contributions to this bill. I 
would also like to thank all the members of the Commerce Committee —in particular, 
the Hon Peseta Sam Lotu -Iiga and Alfred Ngaro —for th eir contributions during the 
select committee process. It is a very important bill, particularly for the people of South 
Auckland, where I have got my office. It is my pleasure to commend this bill to the 
House. 
KRIS FAAFOI (Labour—Mana): Thank you very much for the chance to speak in 
this second reading of the Credit Contracts and Financial Services Law Reform Bill. 
Like the Minister of Pacific Island Affairs, Sam Lotu -Iiga, I also represent a community 
that is disproportionately affected by the kind of behaviour that is carried on by third -
tier lenders—or, as we like to colloquially call them, loan sharks —and the likes of, as I 
guess they would call themselves, mobile traders, whom we like to call truck shops.  
10 Apr 2014 Credit Contracts and Financial Services Law Reform Bill 17213 
It would not seem fair to any fair -minded New Zealander that interest rates of the 
likes of 50 percent to 100 percent, or even more, are charged to vulnerable people in our 
community. I think if you asked any fair -minded New Zealander who wants a fair g o 
for consumers, especially those who are vulnerable and who cannot get credit from the 
likes of traditional banks, they would say that getting charged the likes of 50 to 100 
percent is just not fair. It lands a whole lot of families —and, as I say, there a re a whole 
lot of families in my community who sign up to those kinds of deals —in massive 
trouble. It usually ends up with them going to the likes of the local citizens advice 
bureau or the Porirua Budget Service. I am going to see the Agape Budgeting Serv ice 
tomorrow in Porirua. Those are the kinds of people who end up dealing with the hurt of 
the families because the likes of third -tier lenders, or loan sharks, are able to charge 
exorbitant interest rates.  
Although we are supporting this piece of legisla tion, this is a massive opportunity 
gone for this Government to take some real action to introduce interest rate caps. I do 
want to acknowledge my colleague Carol Beaumont, who has a number of 
Supplementary Order Papers on this bill. One of those specifica lly does do what the 
Government should have done in the introduction of this bill, and that is to look at 
interest rate caps. I think it was Mr Lotu -Iiga who said that these interest rate caps do 
not work. So maybe Mr Lotu -Iiga would like to ask the likes of many countries in 
Europe, Mexico, Canada, South Africa, Japan, Singapore —which has a Government 
that this Government always says is doing a good job financially —the US, Australia, 
and, most recently, the United Kingdom as to why they think it is appropr iate to put in 
interest rate caps for third -tier lenders. I think those Governments probably recognise 
the fact that there is huge public interest in making sure that the most vulnerable in our 
communities are not stung more by the likes of interest rates of 50 percent to 100 
percent.  
Essentially, what we are saying here is that this side of the House is not OK with the 
most vulnerable people in our community going to third -tier lenders and paying interest 
rates of 50 percent to 100 percent or more. But th at side of the House —the 
Government; National, United Future —are quite OK with people who probably cannot 
afford to take out these loans having these huge, exorbitant interest rates. That is exactly 
what this boils down to. We are not OK with it, but that Government is OK with it. 
From now on, all the hurt that the likes of budgeting services see around the country 
can be blamed on that Government because it is quite OK with letting things go on as 
they are now.  
Or, one person in this House, the Hon Peter Dunne, could change his mind again. He 
could change his mind again. Andrew Little said that Mr Dunne supported a member’s 
bill back in 2010 in the name of Carol Beaumont that would have introduced interest 
rate caps. I want to quote from the same letter that Mr Little—

Dunne to change his mind again. His is the one vote that could change this whole thing. 
Peter Dunne said in 2010 that he was OK with interest rate caps, but now that he is back 
in the House with the Government, he is not OK with it.  
So write letters to Peter.Dunne@parliament.govt.nz. Send him a letter —to the Hon 
Peter Dunne. It is freepost. If you are not OK with 50 to 100 percent or more interest 
rates, write Peter Dunne a letter, send him an email, or bombard his office with phone 
calls. He is the one who can change this whole situation. The Government has not 
shown any leadership on this. It is dead against interest rate caps. It does not want to 
introduce them. But there is one person in this House who can change everything.  I fear 
that he may not change his mind, because what did he do with asset sales? He made 
sure he voted for that. That squeaked through with one vote. But I do not want to 
discourage people from trying to get Peter Dunne to change his mind on this.  
Can I just take a brief moment, because this was the first substantive piece of 
legislation that I sat through on the Commerce Committee, to thank other members of 
the Commerce Committee. It was a relatively good process. We had the odd stoush —
nothing compared with what we have had recently. 
Carol Beaumont: Officials. 
KRIS FAAFOI : Can I thank the officials too because, as the chair of the select 
committee, Jonathan Young, said, the bill is very technical, but I think the way the 
officials guided us through this process made it very plain sailing for someone who had 
to make sense of this as a new member to the select committee.  
I do represent a community where the effects of loan sharks and truck shops do have 
a disproportionate effe ct. Although I support this piece of legislation, I do think, as I 
have said before, that we have missed an opportunity to make the lives of those people 
better. I have had people in my office who have been in tears because of the interest 
rates and the debt that they have got themselves into with loan sharks. I cannot do much 
more than offer the services of a budgetary advice service. That is heartbreaking 
because I think this Parliament should be able to do something to prevent people from 
getting into th ose situations. I think an interest rate cap certainly would have been one 
of those ways.  
There is also one person I do want to thank who is not in this House any more, and 
that is Charles Chauvel. Before he left this House he also took a very strong lead ership 
role in the Ōhariu electorate, which Mr Dunne is the MP for, in making sure that this 
issue was brought to the fore. It was actually 5 years ago, when the effects of the global 
financial crisis started kicking in, that this really started to hit home, especially with our 
most vulnerable people in our communities.  
As Sam Lotu-Iiga said, he put in a member’s bill 3 years ago —3 years ago. It was 3 
years ago, and we are sitting here today, 6 months before an election, and something is 
being done about it only now. My ques tion is why it has taken so long for this 
Government to get off its chuff and make sure that something is done for these most 
vulnerable people. We have still got the Committee stage of this debate to go, and I

I just want to finish up with this thing. There is one vote in this House that can 
change it. We on this side of the House are not OK with interest rates of 50 to 100 
percent or more. If this Government does not support the Supplementary Order Paper of
